item.title: Report: NFL considers flexing Eagles-Commanders out of prime time
item.description: As the NFL season begins to take shape, the league office has a growing body of evidence to inform potential flex decisions.
item.content:encoded:
As the NFL season begins to take shape, the league office has a growing body of evidence to inform potential flex decisions. And one game has emerged as a candidate to be the first to exit its current prime-time slot.

Via Rob Tornoe of the Philadelphia Inquirer, the NFL is considering moving the Week 8 game between the Eagles and Commanders out of the Sunday night window.

Plenty of factors influence the NFL's decision-making process. One obvious factor becomes the game that would replace it.

In Week 8, it may not be easy to find a game that would attract a larger audience, even if the Commanders lose to the 49ers on Monday night and fall to 1-4-1 and if the Eagles lose to the Panthers on Sunday and slump to 2-4.

Given the apparent rule that at least one game in each division rivalry must be televised in a Sunday afternoon window, Vikings-Lions, Browns-Steelers, and Chiefs-Broncos would seem to be off limits. Steelers-Browns (Week 4) and Broncos-Chiefs (Week 4) previously were televised in prime time, and the Vikings are scheduled to host the Lions on Sunday night in Week 15.

Of course, the league could decide to take the earlier Vikings-Lions game, with a flex of the Week 15 game in Minneapolis into an afternoon window.

Ravens-Bills becomes a possibility, but the Ravens also play the following Thursday night. The league may not want to give the Ravens seven fewer hours or so between games on a short week.

Colts-Jaguars is a possibility; the Jaguars are 4-1 and the Colts should move to 3-3 this weekend with a home game against the 0-5 Titans. The league would need to consider whether Eagles-Commanders would carry extra national sizzle than Colts-Jaguars even if both Philadelphia and Washington lose this weekend.

Ultimately, the outcomes of this weekend's games will influence the final decision. For now, the Inquirer reports that the possibility of an Eagles-Commanders flex is on the radar screen. The deadline arrives on Tuesday, October 20 — the day after Week 6 ends with the Commanders facing the 49ers in Santa Clara.

item.title: Report: Lamar Jackson has a "realistic chance" to return Week 6
item.description: On Monday, Ravens head coach Jesse Minter told reporters that quarterback Lamar Jackson was "definitely doing better" after missing Week 5 with an ankle injury.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, Ravens head coach Jesse Minter told reporters that quarterback Lamar Jackson was "definitely doing better" after missing Week 5 with an ankle injury.

Now there's an indication he may be back after being sidelined for just one game.

Jackson has a "realistic chance" to play against the Browns on Sunday, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter.

Jackson did not practice last week, but Minter has praised the quarterback for doing everything he can to get back as quickly as possible.

In four games so far this season, Jackson has completed 70.8 percent of his passes for 967 yards with six touchdowns and one interception. He’s also rushed for 144 yards with a TD.

Jackson did not practice last week. The Ravens' first injury report of Week 6 is due out later on Wednesday.

item.title: Seahawks Week 6 power rankings: Close loss to 49ers drops Seattle nearly out of top 5
item.description: The national media is concerned over the Seattle turnovers and run game.
item.content:encoded:
Entering week 5, the Seattle Seahawks bounced back in their power rankings after defeating the Los Angeles Chargers. However, after losing to the San Francisco 49ers, will Seattle fall down those rankings once again? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (BR), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle.

Let’s start with the national sites that were most punishing of Seattle after their loss to the 49ers. B/R, which dropped the Seahawks down from 3rd to 6th, brought up the turnover issues that are plaguing the team. “The Seattle Seahawks are turning the ball over at an alarming rate – nine giveaways over the last four weeks.” Meanwhile, CBS also dropped Seattle down three spots, from 4th to 7th best. In this ranking, CBS mentions that Seattle has to get their running game going as it is the key to their offense working. 

ESPN did drop the Seahawks as well, however they remain in the top five, coming in at number 4th best in the league, one spot down from last week. ESPN noted that the Seahawks have an issue on defense, however that issue happens to be the offense. ESPN mentioned that Seattle has given up 44 points off turnovers, which is tied for most in the NFL. 

Both NFL.com and PFT did not penalize the Seahawks in their rankings despite the loss. PFT, who kept Seattle ranked at number five, stated that “they’re trying too hard to be something other than [what] they were in 2025.” Meanwhile, NFL.com who kept the Seahawks at third best in the NFL, also noted that the Seahawks (specifically Sam Darnold) need to clean up their play. However, NFL.com was also the only national site to maintain positivity over the team, stating that “a narrow loss to the No. 1 team in my rankings doesn’t knock the ‘Hawks down the board.” 

Overall, it is not surprising to see the Seahawks fall down the power rankings after their second loss in three weeks. However, despite the slight slide down, the national media seems to be high on the team despite their turnover and run game concerns. If Seattle can fix those then they will still be a threat for another title run. 

Entering week 5, the average power ranking between the five polled sites was 3.6. Entering Week 6, that average has fallen to an even 5.0. The Seahawks face the Denver Broncos next week on Thursday Night Football. Despite still having an average ranking in the top five, another loss (this time to the Broncos) could really have Seattle fall off of a cliff (at least in the power rankings sense).

item.title: Meet Cam Edge, the QB for the Best Team in HBCU Football
item.description: Edge has the Bears soaring in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
As summer faded to fall, most of those that pay attention the MEAC had one team and one team only circled as the favorite to get to Atlanta and hoist the Celebration Bowl trophy at season’s end. The one that did it last year. South Carolina State, rightfully, garnered most of the preseason attention as not only the best team in their conference but in HBCU football on the whole. Chennis Berry is a heck of a coach and his group has been the standard for several years now.

Fast forward two months, however, and it is not Berry’s Bulldogs that are taking up those same headlines. Instead Morgan State has found itself in that particular spot seven weeks into the 2026 season, much to the surprise of many around FCS football. The Bears, currently holders of a 5-1 overall record, are suddenly vaulted into those same conversations. Exciting come-from-behind wins, a feisty offense that refuses to say die and genuine belief that they are the best team on the field in every game they play; those are the traits of these MSU Bears. And it is their senior quarterback, the one who has willed them to victory after victory, that is the center of it all.

Last week Cameron Edge… or Cam as he likes to be known… calmly walked into the huddle against Robert Morris. There was under five minutes to play and his Bears had just fallen behind by six to the Colonials at home in front of a homecoming crowd of over 11,000. As collected as could be, he proceeded to command an 11-play, 75-yard march that wound up in the end zone with just 22 seconds remaining. Edge completed three passes on that drive before eventually handing the ball off to Keith Jenkins Jr. who did the rest; a final four minutes of a game that so perfectly sums up who he and this Bears team is.

There hasn’t been a pressure that’s been to great for Edge and maybe that’s because he’s taken the long road to get to where he is right now. He’s a story that, at least at its start, is very common in today’s brand of college football. A highly touted recruit that bounced around in the FBS before finding his home… and his niche… at an FCS program that needed his abilities. Edge, though, is not one of the many transfers that has gotten lost into the endless void of the transfer portal and buried behind a mountain of other players and it’s paying dividends for both him and his team.

Edge, a native of Clayton, Delaware, began his college career at Maryland as a four-star quarterback out of Symrna High School. He turned down offers from Oregon, LSU, Penn State, Michigan State and Tennessee to play for the Terps. His action in Maryland, though, was limited. In three seasons, Edge appeared in just four games. His most notable moment was stringing his first college touchdown pass in the 2023 Music City Bowl in Maryland’s 31-13 win over Auburn. Following the 2024 season, in which he completed just five passes for 67 yards, Edge transferred to Eastern Michigan. Last year he rode the bench the entire season for the Eagles. No game time, no live reps.

Going into his senior season, Edge decided to transfer one more time and Morgan State came calling. The Bears went 4-8 last season and the quarterback position was a bit of a revolving door following its conclusion. Between Raymond Moore III, last year’s MEAC Rookie of the Year, leaving for UTEP and Kobe Muassau exhausting his eligibility, MSU needed help at the QB spot. It was clear from the get-go that Edge would be their guy as he was the only quarterback transfer Morgan State brought in during the last cycle.

He’s taken that chance and run with it. Edge’s numbers are excellent six games into the season. He currently leads the MEAC in passing yards (1,337), passing yards per game (222.8) and touchdowns (11). His 68.3% completion rate is also sixth best in the entire FCS. Morgan State is ranked in the STATS Perform national media poll at #24 this week for the first time in program history. They have notable out-of-conference wins over Villanova (who made it all the way to the FCS semifinals last year) as well as Towson and Robert Morris. Their 5-1 start is the best they’ve seen since 2009.

The marriage between Edge and Morgan State has been a fruitful one for both sides so far and the expectations are, understandably, as high as they’ve been in quite sometime over in Baltimore. Edge is already one of just a few players named to the 2027 HBCU Legacy Bowl, an annual senior showcase for HBCU players hoping to get into the pros. The talks of a MEAC title and a Celebration Bowl are not as far-fetched as they once were. Conference play has not yet begun, but Edge and the Bears appear to be the new team to beat.

Morgan State travels to Nashville this weekend to take on Tennessee State at Nissan Stadium for the Tigers homecoming game. It’s another game that they’re favored to win and another opportunity for Edge to continue to show why both he and MSU made the right decision last offseason.

Kickoff is set for 6:30 PM (ET) on Saturday. The game can be streamed on ESPN+.

The Daily Slop – 14 October 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Articles

The Athletic (paywall)

That botched final play: What we know and still don’t know

Daniels could have thrown the ball over Sinnott’s head — or even heaved it downfield, well beyond Okonkwo or Burks — and the clock would have stopped with time remaining.

Instead, after he stumbled on his dropback and made the half-hearted fake to White, Daniels — how should we put this — freaked out. He ran to his left, then fell back to his right, just getting back to the line of scrimmage — where he then sat for about four seconds.

“This is terrible situational awareness,” former fullback Michael Robinson said on NFL Network. “I don’t think Jayden Daniels knew whether he had timeouts or not. Look at the urgency. There was none.

“He was about to lay on the ground. And to me, a picture is worth 1,000 words. Right here, the Washington Commanders did not know what to do in the situation.”

Said Green Bay Packers pass rusher Micah Parsons of Daniels: “There’s no way I’m taking a sack with (12) seconds left and no timeouts. … This is your third year. … You’ve been to the NFC Championship Game. You’ve been in big moments before. And to me, even after a sack, you’re casually getting up.”

Last Man Standig (paywall)

New focus puts the onus on the QB

The quarterback’s decision not to throw the ball away, followed by the offense’s lack of urgency as time expired, produced the lasting images of one of the more baffling endings in franchise history.

Daniels’ role can’t be absolved, regardless of what happened earlier in the chain of command. Quarterbacks are the extension of a coach on the field. The greats have the instincts to know when the information no longer applies to the question presented. As the clock ticked down, the situation demanded an adjustment from Daniels. It never came.

ESPN

Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 6

Daniels, independent of any call from the sideline, is the player holding the football. He knows the clock is running; he knows (or at least should know) he has no timeouts. He simply cannot be tackled in bounds. He has to throw the ball away.

Quinn should not lose his job because Daniels short-circuited on a play he didn’t fully understand. But you can’t really come back from this. It’s Quinn’s third season as the head coach in Washington, and all the magic of Daniels’ rookie year and that deep 2024 playoff run is forgotten. If Washington can’t beat this version of the Giants — up by 14, in the rain, facing a backup quarterback and with a hand-delivered victory at the end of overtime — it’s hard to imagine it’ll beat enough teams to justify keeping the staff. Remember, Quinn made two coordinator changes last offseason. He’s all out of cards to play to keep his seat for another year if things don’t change very quickly.

Why did the Commanders defense struggle so much in the second half vs Giants?

In the first half, they dominated, as they have done a few times this season. The Giants failed to get anything going on the ground and the passing game wasn’t much better. The Giants managed just three points in the first half, but things completely changed in the second half. The Giants scored on every possession in the second half, bar the kneel down on the final play before going to overtime.

Going from conceding just a field goal in the first half, to giving up scores on four consecutive possessions in the second half is quite the change. So what changed? To break that down, we have to start by looking at what went well in the first half. The Giants came out looking to establish the run game, but the Commanders were very stout against the run early on, as they have been most of the season.

To emphasize just how good the Commanders were against the run, after Daniels ran for his first touchdown, the TV broadcast put up a stat that Daniels had a 38-yard run for that touchdown, and at that point the Giants had 37 total rushing yards as a team. And that was midway through the third quarter. So the Giants had nothing going for them on the ground in the first half, which meant they were constantly in second and third and long situations.

So what changed? In the second half, the Giants opted to almost abandon the run game and instead went to plays they would call “extensions of the run game”.

Sports Illustrated

Tress Way Reached a Milestone No Washington Punter Had Before

One franchise milestone was overshadowed by the 27-27 tie this past weekend as punter Tress Way surpassed 40,000 career punting yards. Way became the first punter in franchise history and the 36th in NFL history to reach that mark. Officially, Way and Bryan Anger are the only two active punters above that threshold. Earlier this year, Way played in his 200th game for the Washington Football franchise (Commanders, Redskins, WFT), joining Washington Legends Darrell Green, Monte Coleman, Art Monk, and Dave Butz as the only players to reach that mark in the Burgundy & Gold.

Way was highly active and effective Sunday, punting six times for 312 yards, for a 52-yard gross average and a 43.3-yard net average. His longest punt traveled 59 yards from Washington’s own seven-yard line in the first quarter.

Washington Commanders have add running back to practice squad

Devin Neal is joining the Commanders’ practice squad.

Neal began his career with the New Orleans Saints as a sixth round pick in the 2025 Draft. Neal played sparingly through the first two months of the season before stepping into an elevated role over the final month where he drew at least seven carries in four consecutive games. Neal’s best performance came in the week 14 win against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers after he totaled 70 yards and one touchdown on 19 carries. Neal also recorded touchdowns in each of his final two appearances in 2025.

Neal’s rookie season ended after he totaled 206 yards and two touchdowns on 57 carries, equating to 3.6 yards per carry, while adding 104 receiving yards on 17 catches and 19 targets. Yet his stint in New Orleans was cut short after suffering a hamstring injury during preseason ahead of the 2026 regular season. Neal then joined the Minnesota Vikings’ practice squad after a workout before being waived days later, leading him to now head to Washington exactly one week later in hopes of jumpstarting his NFL career in year two.

Rasul Douglas – Commanders CB

When the Commanders signed Rasul Douglas this offseason, fans approached the move with cautious optimism. He was experienced and physical enough to perform well in Daronte Jones’ scheme, but there’s no telling when age will catch up to veteran cornerbacks.

Thankfully, Douglas has taken on the challenge superbly. He’s now starting opposite Amik Robertson, and he is making a considerable impression. His last two games have been particularly notable, which will only serve him well in pursuit of another deal beyond 2026.

Even with the return of 2025 second-round pick Trey Amos, Douglas still has a role to play. Jones’ defense starts games well but drops off significantly in the second half. That’s a problem, but the Virginia Tech product has quickly emerged as a real positive through the opening five games.

the Cowboys are reportedly hiring a more experienced assistant to pair with Parker as a first-time play-caller: Mike Pettine.

And not only are they bringing the Bucks County, Pennsylvania native into the fold. But the Cowboys are also moving Parker from his normal role on the sideline to the booth.

It’s hard to look at this setup and not think back to when the Eagles bizarrely decided to put Matt Patricia in charge of their defense mid-stream during the 2023 season, effectively demoting Sean Desai in the process without actually formally doing so.

That setup ended up being an abject disaster for the Eagles, who historically collapsed at the end of that season.

Philly Voice

The Eagles should punt on the 2026 season, trade still-valuable players for future assets

[I]f you’re a Birds fan, this season sucks. And, spoiler, it is only going to continue to suck.

However, Howie Roseman and the Eagles are in a position to choose their suckage path the rest of the season. 

The Eagles suck in a way that isn’t likely fixable

The 2026 Eagles O-line, as currently constructed, is one of the worst in the NFL. Of course, the biggest domino to fall in the deconstruction of the line was the unexpected retirement of Lane Johnson last week.

LG Landon Dickerson did not have a good training camp, and he had his worst game as a pro Week 1 against the Commanders. He subsequently went on injured reserve. The Eagles then moved starting C Cam Jurgens to LG, and Drew Kendall filled in at C. 

Jurgens then proceeded to play poorly at LG for three games before he reported concussion symptoms and was traded to the Baltimore Ravens. Meanwhile, Kendall sustained a knee injury and did not play Week 5 in London against the Jaguars.

In the Eagles’ loss in London, Tyler Steen suffered a shoulder injury, but did return to the game.

This is not 2024.

Through five games during the 2024 season, the offense had gained 1,834 yards. They were averaging 366.8 yards per game. This season through five games… 1,311 yards, or 262.2 per game. That would be 104.6 fewer yards per game.

The 2024 offensive line was intact and playing well, and the Eagles had a run game that they could hang their hat on. They at least had an identity to lean into.

Following the Eagles’ Week 4 loss to the Rams, Sirianni acknowledged that the team “obviously” did not yet have an identity.

But more troubling is that it’s hard to figure out anything the offense does well. There’s no identity now, and no identity on the horizon.

The Eagles are unquestionably the most successful team in the NFC the last decade. They should be hunting for Lombardi trophies, not division title banners. Since they are not capable of winning a Super Bowl this season, based on all of the above, they should let the other three loser teams in the division compete for the right to get knocked out of the playoffs in the wildcard round.

left tackle Jordan Mailata wasn’t thinking about moral victories.

Big Blue View

The Giants need to open up their offense and become less predictable

The Giants need to be realistic about the world in which they now live. They desperately want a power running game to be the foundation of their offense. The problem is that the Giants’ running game has just been bad since the loss of Dart. The Giants’ running backs have averaged just 3.49 yards per carry over the last three games, with zero touchdowns and three fumbles.

That is simply not winning football, to the point where the failure to produce combined with the philosophic focus on the run game is actively harming the team.

The problem is that despite having the fourth-highest run rate on neutral downs, the Giants’ -0.2.18 EPA per play on neutral-down runs is among the worst in the NFL.

The Giants’ EPA on dropbacks, meanwhile, is 12th in the NFL at 0.141 per play — just between the Bengals and Packers.

[F]ullback Patrick Ricard was on the field for 22 plays against the Commanders, two of which were penalties. Of the remaining 20 plays, 12 of them were runs and 10 of those were between the tackles.

The Giants had a strong tendency to play out of condensed sets, and then run between the tackles into the teeth of the defense.

[Against Washington], Cam Skattebo ran the ball 13 times and Najee Harris carried the ball 5 times. In each case, most of their carries came in heavy, condensed formations. However, their best carries came when the Giants spread their formation out. In fact, Skattebo’s 19-yard run and 9-yard run both came when the Giants used 11-personnel and wider formations to lighten the box an force Washington to defend more field.

What to do now?

Quite simply, the Giants need to open their offense up, they need to lean into the pass, and they need to help their players.

I want to make it clear that I don’t think the Giants need to turn into the Cowboys and throw 40 times per game.

However, it’s clear that despite Jameis Winston’s history of turnovers and the Giants having a razor-thin depth chart at wide receiver, passing is their better option right now.

Niners Nation

49ers news: We’re on to Washington

The Commanders are a fascinating team. The same guys that beat Seattle also just tied the New York Giants. At 1-3-1, they’ll be desperate to save their spiraling season. A win on national TV against the hottest team in the league would be exactly what the doctor ordered for them.

With Sonny Styles leading the way, their front seven will be a problem. He’s been really really good… maybe one of the few linebackers that can keep up with George Kittle or Christian McCaffrey. Their secondary looks much more exploitable.

On the other side of the ball, their interior offensive line seemed like their biggest vulnerability before the season started. They’ve stabilized by signing Lucas Patrick to play center and getting starting guard Sam Cosmi back from injury. The x-factor, which I’m sure will be talked about ad nauseam, is none other than Jayden Daniels.

Niners Nation

What is the 49ers plan at receiver without Deebo Samuel?

The 49ers have now lost Ricky Pearsall, De’Zhaun Stribling, Christian Kirk, Demarcus Robinson, Samuel, and Khadarel Hodge all to injuries for some period of time.

The 49ers trotted out Brandin Cooks for the first time, while Jacob Cowing played a heavy number of snaps behind Mike Evans. Additionally, we saw Jordan Watkins get 22 snaps as well. Right now, those three are the team’s top depth after Evans, who is still recovering in his own right from a painful rib injury.

What is the 49ers plan at receiver without Samuel?

“Well, yeah, with Deebo out, we have five guys on the roster and Deebo being out, that would be four,“ head coach Kyle Shanahan said about his receivers. So the next guys up to get activated would be one of the three guys on practice squad. Because also in that game Jake went down with an ankle. He ended up being all right, but the numbers got low real quick. That’s why we always like to get five up for game day. We’ve got four guys on our roster, so we’ll most likely decide on one of those guys throughout the week.”

Currently, the 49ers have three receivers on their practice squad: Wesley Grimes, Will Pauling, and Xavier Smith. So will they look for more reinforcements during the week? Shanahan doesn’t believe so, at least for now.

Joe Brady wishes he’d taken two knees before Monday night’s game-winning field goal

Brady expressed regret for attempting the game-winning 45-yard field goal on second down, with two minutes left in overtime.

“I didn’t want to run two QB sneaks with the fall process of, again, getting — putting the ball in harm’s way, taking some shots on Josh, just to get — we knew we were already in line,” Brady said. “So it’s like, hey, do I just, hey, center the ball and just take two knees? You know, you go back two yards, but you don’t give them, you know, they end up worse if you miss. They get 45 seconds to, you know, to go 20 yards for the field goal. Big difference in two-minute, and, you know, the 45-yard field goal and a 47-yard field goal percentages, you should still be good to go, right?

“And, you know, so if I had that opportunity again — look, I was convicted about it. You know, [Tyler Bass] was good to go. The conversation we had in the huddle and upstairs was like, ‘Let’s just go win the game right now.’ But, you know, to not give them that shot again, if we do miss, the best thing would be is to take two knees and say, ‘Hey, the 45 and the 47 is not of big difference.’ Be a completely different story if the ball was a little further back. I’d be no indecision on taking knees if we were a little closer. We were just in that. It is a long field goal. We had just missed an extra point, but had the confidence in [Bass], but that’s when I do wish I probably took two knees, and then we kicked the game winner. And if anything, they’d have 45 seconds and not two minutes.”

Plenty of Bills fans would surely prefer a 45-yard field goal try to a 47-yard field goal attempt. For obvious reasons. Regardless, the thought process is another example of the decisions coaches need to make in real time, with the clock ticking.

If the kick had missed from 47, the Rams would have had less than 40 seconds to gain enough ground to try another potential game-winner. A miss from 45 would have given the Rams triple that amount of time.

item.title: AFC linebacker emerges as potential Rams trade deadline target
item.description: Gray could shore up a weak link in L.A.’s defense
item.content:encoded:
If the Los Angeles Rams want to bolster their defense at the trade deadline, Tennessee Titans linebacker Cedric Gray should be near the top of their wish list.

That’s a position of need for the Rams, while Gray himself has fallen out of favor with the Titans despite an especially productive 2025 campaign.

Los Angeles isn’t necessarily the first destination you think of when it comes to taking a swing on a linebacker. Under coach Sean McVay, the Rams simply have not put much emphasis or capital into building their off-ball linebackers group. But in a year when you’ve already committed to going all-in for a Super Bowl title, there’s no better time than now to take a swing at an oft-neglected spot.

Currently, Nate Landman is the Rams’ best off-ball linebacker, and to his credit he’s a fine player and contributor for defensive coordinator Chris Shula. Overall, he had a good game against the Buffalo Bills on Monday Night Football in Week 5, flashing numerous times throughout the game.

However, his limitations were also on display, such as on a long run by Bills quarterback Josh Allen in overtime when Landman was manning the middle of the field.

He needs help, and the Rams need better depth when Landman isn’t on the field at all. That doesn’t happen often, considering all that’s currently asked of Landman (he played 89% of this week’s defensive snaps), but this would allow Shula to be more flexible with his personnel.

CEDRIC GRAY

For Gray’s part in this, it’s surprising that someone who was so productive just a season ago could now be on the trade block as some outlets have suggested. After all, he set the Titans’ franchise record for tackles in a single season last year with 164 stops, a bright spot in an otherwise miserable year for that franchise.

A new coaching regime in Nashville has led to a much different story in 2026, however. Under the new Titans brain trust of coach Robert Saleh and defensive coordinator Gus Bradley, Gray has only played 44% of the Titans snaps in the four games he’s played. He’s also only been a starter in two of the four games after starting 16 a year ago.

Saleh was asked about Gray’s playing time last week, and it didn’t make the playing time situation any clearer for the third-year pro.

As of now, Cedric does a good job in the run game and pass game. Cody [Barton] is also a very good linebacker, really good communicator. When you look at nickel defense with Cody and Anthony [Hill Jr.], it has been a good combination for us. We’ve been going more dime, so only one linebacker is on the field on third down, so that’s bringing all the snap counts down also. So there’s a combination of different things. We’re doing a lot of different things personnel-wise. We’re playing with five D-linemen on the field several times a game. So, there’s certain things that are bringing both our snap counts down, but overall percentage-wise, it’s going to be similar.

Something worth noting: Saleh and co. didn’t draft Gray. They did draft Hill. These things matter in the NFL.

RAMS LINEBACKER OPTIONS

The Rams also play a lot of dime and don’t need tons of linebackers all on the field at once. What they do need, however, is an influx of talent at the position. It also doesn’t quite match up that Gray can’t play as the dime linebacker if, in Saleh’s own words, Gray is good in both the run and pass games.

We don’t need to oversell the caliber of player here. This isn’t a potential trade for a Fred Warner clone, or prime Brian Urlacher or anything like that. But it would be a talent upgrade at a position of need.

The Rams want to keep up in the NFC arms race after an admittedly disappointing start to the season. The Titans have been brutal to start the year and there’s no light at the end of the tunnel for them for now. If they’re taking on calls on a player like Cedric Gray, it only makes sense for Los Angeles to keep going all in.

item.title: Can the Browns’ offensive line be fixed? Does it need fixing?
item.description: The Jets had a field day getting after the QB and RB in Week 5. What is the Browns problem and can it be fixed?
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns lost to an inferior opponent this past weekend, when mistakes and a huge number of sacksgave the New York Jets a 17-12 victory. This was one team that all Cleveland fans had stuck a “W” on the schedule. The loss put the Browns at 3-2-0 instead of 4-1-0 and a lead in the division.

The Jets had eight sacks. It was a jailbreak on almost every passing down.

RELATED: PLENTY OF BLAME WHEN THE OFFENSE STRUGGLES

Is Cleveland’s offensive line that bad? What happened, and what is the fix? And not during the offseason, but now.

Is this an offensive line issue, or is Browns QB Deshaun Watson to blame, or does it fall on the scheme, system of Todd Monken?

Cleveland currently starts two rookies along their offensive line: LT Spencer Fano and RG Austin Barber. Barber has been inserted for the injured Tevon Jenkins, who remains out with a back issue. Maybe the inclusion of undeveloped players in the lineup can be the source of the blame for the poor play.

Eight sacks. Obviously, something isn’t gelling. The Jets have had a formidable defense for years, with their problems usually on the offensive side of the ball. And they showed that on Sunday. It seemed like every time Watson dropped back to pass, there was a green jersey or two wrecking the pocket.

According to Pro Football Focus (PFF), the Browns offensive line as a whole is ranked #28. Ouch. 

But hold the phone. By PFF’s data, five of those sacks were credited to the offensive line.

Sack #1

Fano is credited with a sack in the first quarter from LB David Bailey when Watson dropped the snap and the pocket went haywire.

Sack #2

On a first down at New York’s 42-yard line with 12:57 left in the second quarter, Watson was back in shotgun, took the snap, and was almost instantly leveled by former Browns draft pick DE Jowon Briggs. What happened was that right off the snap, center Jenkins squared up but did not have a defender to block. At the same time, Barber took on Briggs while MLB Demario Davis came in without any blocker until he met RB Quinshon Judkins.

Judkins’ block of Davis slammed the Jets defender into Barber, who then lost control of Briggs, and Briggs was now free and able to bear hug Watson for the sack.

Sack #3

The third was also in Quarter 2 with 7:05 before the half.

Bailey lined up at left end. Off the snap with Watson in shotgun, NB Brownlee blitzed, and Howard blocked down to take him. Meanwhile, Bailey was completely unblocked and had a free lane that Watson could do nothing about. 

Sack #4

With 13:01 left in the game, Cleveland had a third-and-30 at their own 35-yard line. Bailey came off the snap like a bullet; the new RT, Dawand Jones, could not extend that long paw far enough, and Bailey was all over Watson quickly.

Sack #5

Then, with 2:41 remaining, the Jets rushed six; Jones could not contain Bailey, who had the first shot, and then Watson went down; he had four New York defenders on top of him. Officially, it was Jackson credited with the sack.

One sack was on the tight end.

Early in the fourth quarter, facing a first-and-15 at the midfield stripe, the Jets were up 10-6. Brownlee came off the left side and met TE Harold Fannin. As Brownlee took an inside move, Fannin threw a shoulder at him and then had a straight shot at Watson. The QB tried to throw the ball in the direction of Boston, but the officials had ruled him down.

On this play, the offensive line had provided a beautiful pocket. 

The other two sacks were on Watson.

As the second quarter was winding down, Watson took the ball in shotgun, and the pocket stood up as the Jets only rushed four, then brought a fifth on a delay. Sanders stayed in to block and took out LB Jamien Sherwood. Watson had a window, but held it. He pumped, then brought it in. Meanwhile, Barber has lost control of his man, the blitzing safety Dane Belton. As Watson tried to go to his left and leave the pocket, Belton had a clean shot and decked the quarterback. 

Take the third-and-five play in the first quarter with the Browns on New York’s seven-yard line. Right off the snap, the Jets rushed six. Rocket Sanders was positioned in the backfield and remained in to block. Fano did not strike his defensive end, Darrell Jackson, but instead jumped outside to take on blitzing LB Will McDonald. Sanders would block Jackson. Johnson and Jenkins took on their defenders as usual. But on the rightside, the defensive end crashed down towards the middle, which left blitzing nickelback Jarvis Brownlee with a straight shot to Watson.

Watson had to get rid of the ball quickly and threw it too high for WR Denzel Boston.

Now, how should this formation be changed? The most obvious is to stick a blocking tight end alongside Howard, hit Brownlee as he approached, and then go out for his route. Boston had a small opening, but he would have been open if Watson had time to get off a good pass instead of forcing the throw.

(Editor’s Note: Does the Cleveland roster have a blocking tight end?)

The end result was a field goal instead of six points.

On the game’s final play, the pocket was there with enough time to survey the field. Bailey eventually got loose from Jones and then chased Watson. Now, if everyone was covered, then they were covered. Watson tried to scramble and look downfield since it was a fourth-and-11 play and there wasn’t a chance that Watson could run for that distance. Bailey caught up with him and the game was essentially over.

Offensive line help

Barber is really struggling. On several plays, he is just being pushed out of the way by much stronger men. On the sack with 2:41 left in the game, it was Bailey who made Watson step up, but Jackson completely pushed Barber out of harm’s way as he then smashed into the Browns signalcaller. His pass-blocking grade is pretty good at 64.0.

Fano is playing very well. His pass-blocking grade is an impressive 77.2 so far. He has allowed just nine pressures in five games and has had one penalty accepted. He is ranked #14 out of 72 qualified offensive tackles.

C Elgton Jenkins is the ace of this group and has been exceptional this year, especially with pass protection. His overall PFF grade is 62.6, but his pass-blocking ability has garnered him an 82.4 grade. That is #1 among 33 centers graded this year.

Johnson also has a good pass protection grade of 76.6, but his run blocking needs work, plus he collects laundry, as he has four accepted penalties. But he has allowed zero sacks so far.

At right tackle, Tytus Howard suffered a knee injury in the first quarter against New York and tried to return. His overall PFF grade is 50.3, but his pass-blocking skills are decent at 64.8. In his place, Jones was beaten badly and often by the Jets. If his man, Bailey, was getting to Watson, his actions were making Watson adjust his pocket presence or simply forcing him to leave the pocket entirely.

The bad offensive line play against the Jets was a fair assessment.

Here are a few facts that affected the outcome of the game:

  • Total dropbacks under pressure: 18
  • Total sacks allowed: 8
  • Watson pressures allowed: 5
  • Offensive line pressures allowed: 8
  • RB/TE pressures allowed: 5

The eight pressures the offensive line allowed equate to 44.4%, which was the second-lowest rate in the league over the weekend.

Another body in-line

What would help the offensive line is to have a tight end or two who can actually block.

(Editor’s Note: Maybe don’t make the first editor’s note before reading the whole article, yet here we are with editor’s note #2)

Blake Whiteheart looks to be involved in the blocking game, but he does not remain engaged and often loses his defender. Harold Fannin is a talented receiver, which is why he was drafted after leading the nation in receptions and receiving yards his final year at Bowling Green. But his limited play strength impacts his effectiveness as an in-line blocker. When healthy, Carsen Ryan attempts to center his blocks, but he isn’t built to duke it out in-line.

Simply put, Cleveland needs a body or two who can actually hit somebody and remain on their block. This roster is currently devoid of a tight end who can block.

In training camp, that appeared to be Jack Stoll, who was released on August 20 with an injury settlement and is now on the San Francisco 49ers practice squad. He would be a welcome addition. On the Browns’ practice squad is 6’-7” John Fitzpatrick. He will engage, but his lower-body strength is questionable and limits his in-line blocking. Recently signed Devin Culp is an average blocker who is a bit undersized.

Free agent tight ends that are known for their blocking skills include former Brown Pharaoh Brown (6’-5”, 246 pounds), who is a terrific blocker, Will Dissly (6’-4”, 265 pounds), and Tyree Jackson (6’-7”, 249 pounds).

As far as Cleveland’s running backs staying in, Quinshon Judkins, Jaleel McLaughlin, and Raheim Sanders give it all they have when kept in for that extra blocker. They don’t always read the correct defender to take on, but they engage and put their entire body into the block.  

Do you think the Browns blocking issues can be solved? Is the problem even on the offensive line at all?

item.title: Browns Week 6: Scouting the Baltimore Ravens with a new coach, lots of changes
item.description: The Cleveland Browns are familiar with much about the Baltimore Ravens, but the Week 6 opponent has a lot of changes too
item.content:encoded:
As the Browns look to rebound after a difficult loss at the hands of the New York Jets, the team will prepare for another divisional clash as the Baltimore Ravens come to Cleveland. Like the Browns, the Ravens also underwent a coaching change this past offseason.

It’s the first meeting between the two teams, with the winner having sole possession of 1st place in the AFC North.

New Year, New Harbaugh disciple

It’s well documented that the Baltimore Ravens originally wanted current Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald as their head coach. Macdonald left the Ravens to be the Seahawks’ new head coach, and if he stayed he would’ve been next in line after John Harbaugh. It didn’t happen, but the Ravens decided to settle for Jesse Minter.

Minter, who was on the Michigan Wolverines football staff with current Los Angeles Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh, was the defensive coordinator for the Chargers last season. Minter going from the Chargers to the Ravens felt predictable, but it’s clear why Baltimore coveted him. Minter has put together an impressive staff, with offensive coordinator Declan Doyle evolving into a future head coaching candidate with how Baltimore’s offense has looked this season.

Ravens offense could be better than last season’s

One of the biggest improvements for the Ravens from last season is their offense. Current Browns head coach Todd Monken was able to improve the Ravens’ offense during his tenure, but this year’s looks more potent.

Doyle, who was previously with the Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson, deserves credit. Having an MVP-level quarterback in Lamar Jackson helps. The tandem of Jackson and running back Derrick Henry is one of the best QB/RB tandems in the league.

This is an offense that can generate explosive plays early and often. Wide receiver Zay Flowers is starting to emerge, and rookie tight end Matthew Hibner is becoming a reliable target in the passing game.

Despite an offensive line that’s unsettled in the interior, this is still one of the top offenses in the league.

Baltimore is better than last year, dangerous down the stretch

The only loss the Ravens had this year was to the New Orleans Saints, a game that Baltimore gave away. Outside of that, this team is better than last year’s team. The defense has some concerns but it’s still a unit that is talented.

It seems as if Minter has tapped something into this team that Harbaugh couldn’t do the last two years. In close matchups in previous years, the Ravens would find ways to lose those games, but with wins over the Dallas Cowboys in Brazil and recently with an overtime win over the Atlanta Falcons (minus Lamar Jackson), this team seems to have gotten over their close-game woes.

Baltimore is expected to get healthy, and if they do, this team will be primed for a deep playoff run in a wide-open AFC.

item.title: 3-round Titans mock draft
item.description: Conducting a 3-round Tennessee Titans mock draft in 2027 because they are currently slated to own the No. 1 pick.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans are currently slated to possess the No. 1 overall selection in the 2027 NFL Draft. After Week 5, they are winning the SOS tiebreaker versus the other 0-5 teams (Chargers, Dolphins). The Titans do look like legitimate contenders to earn the top pick, unfortunately.

That has prompted this 3-round Titans mock draft. Titans GM Mike Borgonzi (or someone else?) will have difficult decisions to make if they actually end up owning the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.

Round 1 (No. 1): Jeremiah Smith, WR, Ohio State

Would the Titans draft a quarterback No. 1 overall to replace Cam Ward? Personally, we’re currently unimpressed by this upcoming QB class. Arch Manning and Dante Moore haven’t been good enough. The Titans may have to decide between choosing a QB to replace the current No. 1 overall quarterback, or a wide receiver who makes the rookie fourth overall pick a WR2.

Jeremiah Smith is a generational prospect and the Titans shouldn’t overthink it, if given the opportunity. He looks like a legitimate Hall of Fame talent. Adding Smith to this offense would give Ward even fewer excuses in 2027. If the Titans have to draft a QB in 2028, inheriting Smith is a good problem for that rookie passer to have.

Round 2 (No. 35): Clev Lubin, EDGE, Louisville

Jeffery Simmons is the only Titans pass rusher currently capable of getting after the quarterback. The edge-rushing group is particularly bad. Jermaine Johnson II is on an expiring contract. Femi Oladejo doesn’t look like he’ll ever be more than a rotational player. Keldric Faulk is still growing and developing, but he’s more of a “BIG END” ala Arik Armstead in Robert Saleh’s system as opposed to a game-wrecking pass rusher.

Louisville’s Clev Lubin is an exciting pass rusher. He proved capable of handling better competition by registering 8.5 sacks in 2025 after having 9.5 sacks at Coastal Carolina in 2024. Lubin already has another four sacks in 2026.

Round 3 (No. 66): LJ Martin, RB, BYU

Both Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears are on expiring contracts. The Titans shouldn’t bring either player back in 2027. The offense’s inability to consistently run the football is hurting Cam Ward.

If the Titans decide to give Ward one final opportunity in 2027, they’ll need a significant investment at running back. BYU’s LJ Martin is a good-sized back (6-2, 225) with a three-year period of excellent production. Martin is currently my fifth-ranked RB in this class.
