item.title: Film review: T.J. Sanders made most of 2026 debut with Bills in win vs. Rams
item.description: Sanders showed why he was an early second-round pick with his performance vs. Rams
item.content:encoded:
T.J. Sanders made a darn-good first impression in his sophomore season debut for the Buffalo Bills in their win over the Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 5.

He played 51 snaps in Los Angeles, easily the most of his NFL career to date, and made impactful plays against the run and pass throughout the contest.

The man I labeled as “the ultimate X-factor” on Buffalo’s defense before the season was credited with five tackles, two stops, and one pressure against the Rams.

Let’s dive into what the film showed about his performance.

Sanders go-to move is a violent swipe. That was the case at South Carolina, and he’s brought it with him to the NFL. He often adds a little crossover wiggle to really sell it, and his hands are powerful.

As a rookie, because his pad level would rise when attempting that move, he’d get driven out of the running lane too easily.

Watch here how he’s was able to reestablish his ground to counter off his swipe to find Kyren Williams and stop him for a short gain. Sanders was aligned between the left guard and left tackle at the snap:

As he was starting to get driven back by the left guard, he planted his foot, then worked back to the outside gap to close the intended path for Williams in a flash. Textbook.

Sanders’ strength improvement was noticeable in this contest. Watch here how, when aligned again between the left guard and left tackle, he absorbed the down block from the tight end, anchored, then applied his natural slipperiness to get back to the ball carrier to help out with the tackle:

Not a glorious rep, but defensive tackles are often washed down the line of scrimmage by smaller tight ends because they don’t feel the initial contact and struggle to slow their momentum as they’re attempting to beat the block. Not there for Sanders.

Even when he was driven back off the line of scrimmage, he demonstrated the importance of hand work and explosiveness at defensive tackle.

Aligned at 3T on the outside shoulder of the right guard, watch how Kevin Dotson — with the help of a quick double — does reset the line of scrimmage. That was before Sanders tossed the large, veteran guard aside to free himself to make another impact stop against the run:

Dotson is listed at 6’4” and 328 pounds. Sanders worked through him with relative ease there and exploded to the football.

And if you want classic teaching tape on how to “two-gap” up front, something Sanders almost never did at South Carolina, watch this tackle on Williams. Notice how Sanders’ peaked into the gap off his left shoulder as he stacked the blocker, didn’t see the runner, then shed the block to the other gap, off his right shoulder, while making the tackle:

Two gaps occupied. Two gaps surveilled. Two gaps locked down.

While I can’t totally blame the Rams because it was his season debut and Deone Walker and Greg Rousseau are total physical freaks playing excellent football, Sean McVay’s group had no qualms about attempting to block Sanders with a tight end in this game.

Rarely did that endeavor go well for Los Angeles:

Watch Sanders here, aligned just to the left of Walker at the snap:

Absorb the block. Extend the arms, then work off the block to the football.

That rep is the ideal time to remind you not only of Sanders’ natural athletic gifts — 75th percentile vertical and 84th percentile broad jump — but his length. He doesn’t have tentacles for arms, yet Sanders 80 7/8-inch wingspan placed in the 64th percentile among interior defensive linemen at the combine since 1999. He regularly uses that length well.

And I’ve saved the best for last. For as run and low-key critical run-stopping play is for defensive tackles, in today’s NFL, the largest value comes from pass-rush ability.

Sanders’ sack of Matthew Stafford on the Rams’ two-point conversion attempt was as high-caliber of a rep as it gets at defensive tackle.

Watch him deploy that nasty swipe on the right guard here, and take note of his explosiveness through the line, ability to bend as Stafford attempted to escape, and finishing ability to take the quarterback to the turf:

So let’s call it two pressures on 37 pass-rush snaps for Sanders in this game.

The Bills should be thrilled with the performance the 2025 second-round pick provided in his first action of the 2026 season. And he appeared well conditioned on his 50-plus snaps. His added strength was noticeable. And the explosiveness and hand-work combo jumped off the screen.

Good news for a Buffalo defense that right now is heavily leaning on its front to cause disruption.

item.title: First-place Giants are a distant third in betting odds to win the NFC East
item.description: In seven of the NFL's eight divisions, the team that is currently in first place is also currently the betting favorite to win the division.
item.content:encoded:
In seven of the NFL's eight divisions, the team that is currently in first place is also currently the betting favorite to win the division. The NFC East is the exception.

At 3-1-1, the Giants are in first place in the NFC East by 1.5 games. But they're a distant third in the betting odds to win the division.

The betting odds currently list the 2-3 Eagles as the favorites at +170, followed closely by the 2-3 Cowboys at +180. The Giants are third at +320, and the 1-3-1 Commanders are last at +750.

It's not hard to understand why the bettors aren't sold on the Giants: Despite managing to win three games, they haven't looked particularly good while doing so, on either offense or defense. (Their special teams are playing well.) Starting quarterback Jaxson Dart is out for the season and there are doubts about how long they can keep winning with Jameis Winston. And their schedule has been easy; all five teams they've played currently have losing records.

The schedule stays easy this week, with a home game against the 1-4 Saints. The Giants are 1.5-point underdogs, which underscores how little faith the bettors have in them. If the Giants manage to win on Sunday, their odds to win the division may improve a little. But it won't be until November 8, when they travel to Philadelphia to take on the Eagles, when the Giants can make a statement that they really are the best team in the NFC East. Unless the Giants keep winning through that game, they're going to stay long shots to win the division.

item.title: Terry Bradshaw hints at retirement, says his time as an NFL analyst is 'coming to an end'
item.description: Terry Bradshaw has been a mainstay at Fox for over three decades.
item.content:encoded:
One of the most well-known faces on NFL Sundays knows he's closing in on the end of his career. Long-time NFL analyst Terry Bradshaw hinted at retirement Tuesday, telling "NBC News Daily" he knows his "time on television as a sports broadcaster is coming to an end."

Bradshaw, 78, appeared on the program discussing his new memoir, which is titled "Looking for Terry." During the interview, Bradshaw was asked about his busy schedule, which is when he said he was nearing the end of his broadcasting journey.

While Bradshaw did not reveal his retirement plans, he will be a significant loss whenever he decides to step away from his current role. After a Hall of Fame playing career — one that saw Bradshaw win four Super Bowls — the quarterback immediately signed a broadcasting deal with CBS in 1984. He was an in-game analyst with the network for years before eventually joining its pregame program in 1990.

Four years later, Bradshaw left the network for the same gig at Fox, where he's remained ever since. Over the years, Bradshaw has established himself as a staple of the network's pregame show "Fox NFL Sunday" where he appears in studio alongside Howie Long, Curt Menefee, Michael Strahan and many others.

While Bradshaw is known for his affable personality, his memoir — which was released Tuesday — focuses on his depression diagnosis, struggles with cancer and failed marriages. The broadcaster said that subject matter made his book a tough sell to publishers, who only wanted to hear stories about football.

For now, Bradshaw is still sharing those stories with fans every Sunday. While his retirement might not be imminent, the long-time analyst knows his on-camera time is approaching its end.

item.title: Mailbag: How much of a difference can Cade Mays, Brian Branch make?
item.description: We discuss the impact of the return of Brian Branch and Cade Mays in this week’s Detroit Lions mailbag.
item.content:encoded:
When the Detroit Lions return from the bye, they could have two very important pieces ready to make their 2026 debut. Center Cade Mays, the Lions’ prized offseason signing, appears close to returning from a fractured wrist suffered in training camp. Safety Brian Branch has been champing at the bit to get back on the field after a torn Achilles ended his previous season in early December.

The Lions could really use both players, but how will they use them, and how much of an impact can either make?

That’s one of the main topics on this week’s Midweek Mailbag podcast. But let’s get into it a little in this space.

Starting with Mays, the Lions are faced with an interesting conundrum. Mays’ replacement, Juice Scruggs, has been playing at a pretty high level in his absence. PFF actually has him as the highest-graded center in football, although that doesn’t quite pass the eye test. Still, even coach Dan Campbell has praised Scruggs’ growth at the position over the past month.

“I feel like Juice has gotten better playing center, just getting more comfortable, particularly on the road, silent count, making the IDs, all that,” Campbell said.

So what do they do with Scruggs? Where does Mays provide an upgrade? Will the Lions have to worry about chemistry restarting with Mays in the lineup?

Plus, there was one interesting thing that Campbell said about returning Mays to the lineup that may question the timing of his activation.

“We’ve got to see exactly where he’s at. We’ve got basically two days of half practices with him and so let’s see what it looks like next week,” Campbell said. “He’s going to continue to train here and then we got to make a decision on how do we work this. That’s what’s a little unique, he plays center. It’s not like you’re rotating a guard. So how do we handle this? What’s the best way? Can he go 70 reps? So, there’s a lot of factors that go into it right now.”

Does that mean we get one more week of Scruggs? Could the Lions hold off Mays’ return longer than expected? We discuss it all on this week’s pod.

As for Branch, I don’t think there’s much question that Detroit wants him out there ASAP to help a struggling and beat-up safety room. Detroit hasn’t had much answers on the back end. Things got so dire that Detroit played fifth-round cornerback Keith Abney at safety last week—and it seemed to actually settle things down a bit.

So what will that room like upon Branch’s return? Will Branch go back to his nickle/safety hybrid role, or do the Lions need so much help at the deep, single-high spot that they put Branch there? And who will be playing aside him? And how much of a difference can he truly make?

We tackle those topics, plus:

  • Are the Lions in a better spot at cornerback now?
  • Why are the Lions still bad at third-down offense?
  • Should the Lions be playing more young players on defense? (e.g. Derrick Moore)
  • What’s with the slow starts on offense?
  • What’s the diference between a good kick and punt returner? Who could win those jobs after Tom Kennedy’s injury?

Catch this week’s episode on your favorite podcast platform by searching “Pride of Detroit” or just using the embedded Spotify player below.

If you want even more Lions mailbag content, be sure to watch this week’s episode on our YouTube channel and/or Twitch page. There we have a bunch more between-segments content.

item.title: Liam Coen: I can do more to avoid delay of game penalties
item.description: The Jaguars were able to take advantage of the Eagles' poor clock management to pull out a win at the end of last Sunday's game in London, but their own miscues cost them a chance to take firmer control of the game earlier in the fourth quarter.
item.content:encoded:
The Jaguars were able to take advantage of the Eagles' poor clock management to pull out a win at the end of last Sunday's game in London, but their own miscues cost them a chance to take firmer control of the game earlier in the fourth quarter.

A Trevor Lawrence pass to tight end Brenton Strange landed the Jaguars at the Eagles' 1-yard-line with under nine minutes to play, but they burned a timeout before getting the next snap off. After a false start and a short run, the Jaguars sandwiched a pair of delay of game penalties around an incompletion and ultimately failed on fourth down to end the drive without any points.

The Jags had another delay of game in the first quarter and head coach Liam Coen said on Wednesday that the penalties were "directly on me." He also explained how he can do more to make sure that the Jaguars don't continue to struggle with getting plays off in time.

"That was probably one of the louder atmospheres I've been in a while," Coen said, via Michael DiRocco of ESPN.com. "Especially in those critical moments to where, 'Hey guys, I can help you out with my playcall.' Maybe shorten it up, trim the verbiage or call something a little bit more simplified down there where it was in that end zone specifically that got loud and some of those critical downs."

The Jaguars had 13 penalties overall against the Eagles and they had 13 more against the Bengals in Week 4. They won that game as well, but the lack of discipline is something that is likely to catch up with them if Coen can't clean up the operation in the coming weeks.

item.title: The Packers fixed their most serious problem, and Jordan Love is the biggest winner
item.description: After three weeks of the 2026 NFL season, the Green Bay Packers were 1-2, coming off an embarrassing 35-14 loss to the Atlanta Falcons in primetime, and their issues were clear. The offensive line. Quarterback Jordan Love had been pressured from quite literally the first offensive snap of the season, through the end of that […]
item.content:encoded:
After three weeks of the 2026 NFL season, the Green Bay Packers were 1-2, coming off an embarrassing 35-14 loss to the Atlanta Falcons in primetime, and their issues were clear.

The offensive line.

Quarterback Jordan Love had been pressured from quite literally the first offensive snap of the season, through the end of that Thursday Night Football game against Atlanta at home. The numbers and charting data backed that up, as through the first two weeks Love had been pressured on 44.4% of his dropbacks, behind only Bryce Young, Caleb Williams, and Deshaun Watson, as charted by Pro Football Focus.

And on those dropbacks, Love had completed just 36% of his passes for 300 yards, zero touchdowns, and a pair of interceptions.

That led to some additions along the offensive line, as the Packers came out of that Thursday-night loss and entered something of a mini bye week. Green Bay added Laken Tomlinson, Mekhi Becton, and Kevin Zeitler, a trio of veterans, to help bolster the group.

Tomlinson slid into the starting lineup for Green Bay’s Week 4 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, getting the start at left guard. While he has been the only one of the three additions to see the field — Becton remains on the practice squad and Zeitler, who was active for Week 5 against the Chicago Bears, was behind Travis Glover on the depth chart for that game — the offensive line has seemingly turned the corner.

Consider this. While Love was one of the most pressured quarterbacks in the NFL through Week 3, since then the narrative has completely changed. Over Weeks 4 and 5, Love was pressured on just 13 of his 65 dropbacks, or 20%, according to Pro Football Focus.

Out of the 34 quarterbacks who played over Weeks 4 and 5, that was the lowest percentage rate around the entire NFL.

And it is not as if Matt LaFleur and the Packers coaching staff suddenly leaned into a horizontal passing game, in an effort to get the ball out of Love’s hands quickly. Over this recent two-game stretch, Love has attempted 13 passes of 20 yards downfield or more, deeper route concepts that require more time in the pocket.

Only Jameis Winston has attempted more.

To drive this point home, consider the very first play the Packers ran on Sunday against the Bears. Backed up in their own end of the field, with Love lining up quite literally in the shadow of the end zone and the goalposts, LaFleur and offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich called for a … slow-developing flea-flicker ending with a screen to tight end Tucker Kraft:

Not exactly lacking confidence in the protection when you have this at the top of the game script.

Stenavich had this to say about that play on Tuesday when he met with media in Green Bay:

The Packers first reached the end zone on this deep shot to Christian Watson, working off play-action. We’ll return to that point in a moment but first, watch Tomlinson on the interior, first by helping center Sean Rhyan, and then helping left tackle Jordan Morgan, hold up in protection:

The Bears actually bring pressure on this play, blitzing both Tyrique Stevenson and Jaylon Johnson off the edges, but the line holds up just enough for Love to make the Chicago defense pay.

Love again punishes the Chicago defense on this vertical shot to Watson, who splits the two-deep safeties. The route concept, with a trio of vertical routes to the left side of the formation, tasks linebacker D’Marco Jackson with trying to “carry” Watson’s vertical route, and help the Cover 2 safeties in the middle of the field as the wide receiver splits them.

The quarterback, after a quick fake toss, sees the coverage and gets his eyes right to Watson, as the protection holds in front of him:

Now as noted above, it is time to return to the play-action elements at work here. All three of these examples contain some level of run action — a flea-flicker, a run fake, and then a fake toss on the third snap.

Through the first three weeks of the season, Love and the Packers used play-action on 18.8% of his dropbacks, which ranked just 35th out of 37 qualified passers. Only Jalen Hurts and Cooper Rush used play-action less over Weeks 1 through 3, as charted by Pro Football Focus.

These past two weeks?

Love has used play-action on 30.6% of his dropbacks, ranking 13th in the league over that stretch. And on those plays, Love has completed 25-of-32 passes for 424 yards (a completion percentage of 78.1%) and three touchdowns, without an interception. He has also averaged 13.3 yards per attempt, second to only Lamar Jackson over the past two weeks.

Against Chicago alone, 41.2% of his passing plays were on play-action, and Love went 12-for-14 for 245 yards and a touchdown.

So these concepts have, seemingly, helped.

But sometimes, you just need to block some guys, and your quarterback needs to finally feel comfortable stepping up in the pocket:

The Bears bring a … we can call it a slow-developing stunt here. But the offensive line picks it up, Love feels comfortable stepping up in the pocket (something that was missing earlier in the season) and the Packers are in the end zone again on an absolute heat-check of a throw.

After a tough start, the Packers seem to have found their footing, particularly up front along the offensive line. And they have also identified some concepts in the passing game that have helped to slow the rush across from them, and create some explosive plays in the passing game.

And they are finding their best five to put out there in front of Jordan Love:

There is an old adage about the NFL, that you find out what you are not doing well in September, fix it in October, and prepare for a stretch run in November and December.

It seems like the Packers have checked those first two items off the to-do list.

item.title: Panthers vs Eagles: Storylines to watch
item.description: Breaking down the key storylines to follow in this week’s preview of Panthers vs Eagles
item.content:encoded:
Hello CSR! We’re rocking and rolling into another game week as the 2-2 Panthers are coming off a bye and traveling to Philadelphia for a battle against the 2-3 Eagles. The Eagles started off 2-0 to begin the season but have since lost 3 straight games as they too have experienced the injury bug and shuffling of their roster. OT Lane Johnson abruptly retired last week, they then traded C Cam Jurgens, and they’ve been dealing with multiple injuries at RB including Saquon Barkley, and were missing WR Devonta Smith last week. Those two specifically could be back this week, which might provide a boost to an offense that has struggled MIGHTILY ass season. The Panthers have been dealing with several issues of their own, but could be getting back OT Taylor Moton, DT Turk Wharton, and RB Trevor Etienne this week from their own injury absences. We won’t know the status on any of these guys until much closer to the game, but we can still evaluate the storylines going into the game now.

Offense: Dealing with the Eagles front, specifically Jalen Carter

The Eagles could also be missing EDGE players Jalyx Hunt and Jonathan Greenard, but this is still a pretty strong unit that the Panthers beat up offensive line will be facing this week. They have LBs Zach Baun and Jihaad Campbell manning the front behind DL Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and EDGE Nolan Smith Jr. Jalen Carter in particular could be a massive problem for this Panthers front, whether he lines up in the interior or on the outside. Carter can be extremely disruptive, causing 3 sacks and forcing 3 fumbles already this season, and for a Panthers unit that is playing well in the passing game but still allowing a ton of pressures on Bryce Young, Carter could very much be the X-Factor for this game plan. I don’t know how the Panthers will contain him, especially if both Taylor Moton and Monroe Freeling can’t play, and I didn’t necessarily like the matchup even if one of those two guys is playing. Brad Idzik could elect to again hammer the RPO plays to give Bryce Young some quick completions like they did against the Lions front seven, but the Eagles secondary is considerably better than the beat up unit that Detroit fielded.

Defense: Contain Jalen Hurts

The common denominator in both of the Panthers losses this season was facing a mobile quarterback. While week 1 was an all around bad defensive effort, the Panthers defense has done a relatively solid job in the other 3 games. However, when they faced the Browns, Deshaun Watson’s ability to extend plays and break contain was ultimately the downfall of the defense, who again weren’t “bad”, but those scrambles by Watson were back breaking when the defense was attempting to get off the field. Things won’t get any easier this week, as Hurts can definitely run and likely will since the rest of the offense for the Eagles has very much struggled to get much going. If there’s ever a game for the defense to clean up the issues with containing the quarterback and preventing scrambles, its this one. Having Devin Lloyd back will certainly help, but he can’t do it all and he very much needs the edge defenders to do their job.

Bonus storyline: The plan at cornerback

While the Panthers walked away with a win against a very productive Detroit offense in week 4, their cornerbacks got targeted quite a bit, specifically Akayleb Evans. Now, nobody expected both Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn to go down in the same game the week prior, but the Panthers didn’t really change the formula too much during their bye week. Will Lee, Evans, and Chau Smith-Wade still are the only cornerbacks on the active roster, and they did some churning on the practice squad and have 5 guys eligible to be promoted to the game day roster there. The Eagles have some speedy options between the always reliable Devonta Smith, Makai Lemon, and some of their other depth. The passing offense for them hasn’t been great for several weeks, but Nick Sirianni may choose to let Jalen Hurts put some air yards out there to try and get their offense back on some sort of schedule. Ejiro Evero will need a plan to limit the big plays, and obviously their safety room will play into the equation as well.

What are you watching for this week, Panthers fans?

item.title: We have a lot to break down on the flag front from Bills-Rams
item.description: There were flags galore in Bills-Rams on MNF
item.content:encoded:
If you’re looking for video this week, don’t expect a long one. The data entry and bookkeeping this week alone was a chore. I have a quick one to cover one thing I wanted to emphasize and I also made a really slick looking graphic to help explain why one person was flagged for hitting a defenseless player and another guy wasn’t. You’ll want to stay tuned, I don’t think you’ll find a more hyper-realistic drawing than the one I made for this.

Standard and Advanced Metrics

Penalty Counts

Do you want to hear something incredibly shocking? The Bills, even after this performance and a few shaky ones before it with flags, are only sixth highest in flags called and seventh in flags assessed. I don’t think I need to dissect these charts very much as they’re glaringly obvious. One more fact I suppose. You can’t really blame overtime for this either, as only one flag was called in the “fifth quarter.”

Penalty Yards

None of this is shocking either. When you’re blowing apart the league average in count, it stands to reason the yards will follow. The Bills added 36 yards negated to their total which sounds like a lot but when you have over a dozen flags, it’s to be expected really.

Penalty Harm

Los Angeles Rams

I’ll jump to the a spoiler and say that, despite high counts, neither the Los Angeles Rams or the Buffalo Bills set any records in this game. Not even close. A large part of this was the high volume of “boo-boo” or nuisance flags. Of the 24 total, eight or 33% were false starts. And few of the flags have a crazy story to tell. Here are a few highlights though:

  • Trent McDuffie’s illegal contact scored an extra 1.0 Harm for negating a ten-yard sack. Buffalo winded up with a field goal so that’s not a crazy swing, BUT it would have been Aaron Donald’s first sack of the season and McDuffie screwed him out of it which is kinda funny.
  • Quentin Lake’s defensive pass interference was just the yards, occurring on first down. That said, it was 1st & 20 due to a pass interference flag on Jackson Hawes. On the same drive, Tylan Grable had a false start on 3rd & 8 to give Buffalo 3rd & 13. Josh Wallace’s defensive holding flag only cost the Rams two yards per traditional stats but without it, the Bills are 4th & 4 at the goal line and may not have gotten the touchdown the drive ended. Two mid-tier Rams flags kept that drive going.
  • While those flags arguably gave Buffalo points, Tyler Higbee might have cost his team some. His offensive holding flag came on 2nd & 3 and negated a nine-yard gain. The Rams didn’t convert afterward and attempted a field goal. The one Harrison Mevis missed. Well the one he missed that wasn’t blocked.

It’s pretty wild, but per the Harm metric, the Rams only accumulated 13.2 total, which is beyond the Bad Day line of 10.0 but not horrifically so. By that measure, the suggestion is that flags had a significant but not overwhelming impact on their day. I think that’s pretty fair.

Buffalo Bills

The Bills on the other hand nearly doubled the Bad Day line and hit 19.8 Harm. Let’s see if their flags warrant that “very bad day” suggestion. Let’s just rattle off everything from Jackson Hawes’ 1.7 and the higher ones.

  • I already alluded to Hawes’ flag which wiped out a 7-yard catch by Keon Coleman. This could have cost the Bills a touchdown if they hadn’t been bailed out as noted above.
  • Like the Jackson Hawes’ flag, Tylan Grable’s holding call wiped out a 17-yard pickup by Coleman, so screwing Coleman out of his resurgent stats was a theme for the day.
  • Michael Hoecht was called for a neutral zone infraction which gave up two free downs thanks to happening on third down. This is a question mark flag. On 3rd & 4, the play never happened so we’ll never know if the Rams convert or not. On the rest of the night they went 50% so I’m not about to say the Bills get a stop without this flag, but it’s possible. This drive resulted in a Los Angeles touchdown.
  • C.J. Gardner-Johnson was called for unnecessary roughness (see my graphic below). It gave up a free first down in addition to the 15 yards for 2.5 Harm. The Rams would have been 3rd & 16 and again, I won’t remotely say with any confidence the Bills get a stop, but they might have here. That said, they did get a stop later anyway.
  • Skyler Bell’s offensive holding call looked like it might doom the Bills at the time. On 2nd & 7, Ty Johnson gained 10. That was called back for a total swing of 20 yards and the one down from the first he gained. Khalil Shakir converted the long second down right away and the Bills were in business. Until the next play and James Cook fumbled again. Woof.

Last but not least, I want to address an elephant in the room. While I think the vast majority of Scotta Novak and crew’s calls were the right ones, there were some notable misses. A critical missed defensive pass interference I’m sure you’ve all seen, but I also want to call out the Cole Bishop DPI which I think was just as bad a miss in the other direction. This is the one video I felt compelled to make with shorter time to do things this week.

I thought this live, but slowing it down with all the angles solidified my conclusion. Bishop makes contact, but I don’t see any indication it’s the reason Higbee’s body turns. I think his movement is entirely trying to make the catch and I really dislike the call on Bishop here. The game had enough delays, and adding a bad call into the mix… ugh.

I have one more thing!

Extra fun!

I don’t think I need to bring up the video, but there was a LOOOOOOOT of confusion on two plays and I think I have a slick graphic to clear things up. C.J. Gardner-Johnson was called for unnecessary roughness for hitting a player making a catch while falling. I don’t think anyone is arguing it was helmet-to-helmet which should make things easier. A near flag against a defenseless Matthew Stafford was picked up and I don’t think anyone is arguing that it was shoulder-to-shoulder, which should make things easier.

I heard all sorts of the same things I usually hear with these flags and I want to make things as easy as possible. There are a few ways for a player to be defenseless, but to keep things short here; players that are or just threw a pass, and players making a catch are both considered defenseless. So now for the simple graphic.

Flags on defenseless players are actually VERY simple. If there was forcible contact to specific areas of the player’s body, and the contact was initiated by specific parts of the other player’s body, it’s a flag. OK, that sounds confusing, let’s do the graphic.

Now, I love me some color theory and I needed to make “yellow” for a flag, so bear in mind we’re mixing light not paint. So this is technically correct, the best kind of correct. Green and red make yellow.

The player on the left is defenseless. The green portions of his body are the “no no spots.” In the rulebook that’s the head and neck area. Usually this does not extend to the players shoulders so think head, neck, clavicle right below the neck, and upper spine basically. My photorealistic graphic captures it. The “no no spots.”

The rule book says the other player can’t hit with their helmet/head, shoulder, or forearms. If the red areas or “trouble spots” touch the “no no” spots in a forcible manner on a defenseless player it’s a flag. Green and red make yellow when forcibly smashed together.

That’s all there is to it. Literally. “What else was Gardner-Johnson supposed to do?” Completely irrelevant. All that matters is what did happen. I covered strict liability already this year, but I think the “no no spots” graphic is easier.

Next time you see a defenseless player, think green and red make yellow. Don’t smash your “trouble spots” into a defenseless player’s “no no spots.” Simple!

C.J. Gardner Johnson didn’t follow that rule, Greg Rousseau did.

item.title: Scouting the Enemy: Seattle Seahawks
item.description: The Denver Broncos will battle the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football. Here is a deeper look at their Week 6 opponent.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 regular season rolls on for the Denver Broncos and so does their gauntlet schedule of opponents. On Thursday Night Football, the Broncos will host the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. Here is a deeper look at their Week 6 opponent.

2025 Seattle Seahawks Season Review

The Seattle Seahawks finished the 2025 regular season as the NFC West champions with a 14-3 record. They had top 3 units on offense and defense and went on to defeat the New England Patriots in Super Bowl LX.

2026 Seattle Seahawks Offseason Additions and Departures

When you win the Super Bowl, it’s hard to keep all your good players in the fold the following season. Seattle was no exception and lost a handful of quality contributors during the free agent period.

Defensive backs Riq Woolen and Coby Bryant headed to the NFC in free agency earning big contracts, while edge rusher Boye Mafe signed with the Cincinnati Bengals. On offense, Kenneth Walker III, last year’s Super Bowl MVP, earned himself a huge payday from the Kansas City Chiefs and has revitalized their rushing attack.

The Seahawks made some modest additions in free agency, but most of their remaining salary cap space was dedicated to extending defensive lineman Leonard Wililams, cornerback Devon Witherspoon, and edge rusher Derick Hall.

The Seahawks had eight selections in the 2026 NFL Draft. Unfortunately, their top two picks are injured and most of their rookie class isn’t seeing any playing time. Rookie running back Jadarian Price suffered a chest injury in the third game of the year and is on injured reserve. Bud Clark, the tenacious TCU safety they selected in the second round, broke his ankle in the preseason versus the Tennessee Titans.

Offensive X-Factor: Wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba

In his fourth season with the Seahawks, wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba has solidified himself as one of the best receivers in the National Football League. Heck, he might just be one of the best players in football. Smith-Njigba has posted back-to-back seasons of at least 100 catches. Last season, he won the Offensive Player of the Year honors after he reeled in 119 catches for 1,793 yards and 10 touchdowns.

Five games into the season, and the former first-round pick is on pace to blow away those numbers. He already has 37 catches, 583 receiving yards, and 7 touchdowns. Of those 37 catches, 28 have resulted in a first down or a touchdown. Currently, he is averaging 117 yards per game receiving.

Quite simply, Smith-Njigba has been dominant to start the season. He already has four games with at least 100 receiving yards. He is certainly the player the Broncos’ defense is going to have their hands full trying to limit the most—especially with multiple starters out in their secondary for the second straight week.

Defensive X-Factor: Defensive lineman Byron Murphy

The Seahawks boast one of the best defenses in the National Football League. They’re a top-flight unit against the pass, force a lot of turnovers, and limit big play ability when defending against the run. It’s hard to pinpoint a weak spot in their defensive lineup. Their defensive line is stout, they’re secondary is making a lot of plays, and their linebackers can cover a lot of ground.

The Broncos haven’t performed that great in the trenches thus far. Thursday night’s primetime matchup will be another big test for them. One underrated player for Seattle is third year defensive lineman Byron Murphy. After a relatively quiet rookie season in 2024, the former Texas Longhorns standout started every game last season and put up 62 tackles, 7 tackles for loss, 7 sacks, and 13 quarterback hits.

This year, Murphy is picking up where he left off. He already has 18 tackles, 5 tackles for loss, 5 quarterback hits, and 3 sacks. He is an ascending player and one of the best young interior defensive linemen in all of football. Denver’s interior offensive line is going to have their work cut out combating him and long-time veteran Leonard Williams. They are good against the run and the pass, so Denver’s guys up front better be prepared.

How the Broncos can secure a victory over the Seahawks

I usually try to be optimistic about Denver’s chances most weeks. Alas, this gridiron matchup is one where I’m struggling to find ways for them to win. We all know the Broncos are struggling on offense. It would be a big leap of faith to believe they’ll get back on track against a defense that creates a lot of turnovers and limits big plays down the field.

However, they may have a path if their defense can come up big like they did against the Los Angeles Chargers. Limiting Smith-Njigba will be their biggest test. Though quarterback Sam Darnold hasn’t played well since returning from injury and their run game is struggling. If the Broncos defense can force a few turnovers, that would give them a fighting chance.

At the end of the day, I do expect the Seahawks to win. They’re just a tough draw at this juncture for the Broncos who can’t seem to figure out the right recipe for success offensively.

Hart’s Prediction: Seahawks, 27, Broncos 17.

item.title: Chicago Bears Midweek Musings: Hello Darkness, My Old Friend
item.description: Check out @gridironborn’s midweek musings, including thoughts on Tyson Bagent, Khalil Mack, the Falcons and more.
item.content:encoded:
Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again:

Have you ever watched a movie, hated it, then found yourself watching it again and again? Maybe it’s a popular movie that was always on when you were growing up that didn’t hit you right or something your spouse loves to put on regularly that just isn’t in your genre. You find yourself watching a few minutes before you think – “I’ve seen this movie before… I hate this movie, I need to get out of here”? That’s watching the Bears go to Lambeau for the vast majority of my life. Same movie with a rotating cast of characters, like endless additions to the Night of the Living Dead franchise where no one escapes, and the zombies always win. It’s boring, and I’m ready for a new series to start for real when our protagonist gets back healthy.

For those that may have never spent time in Wisconsin, my experience is that the default side next to a burger or sandwich is cheese curds instead of fries. Might be the only time fries would be considered the healthier side option.

I mentioned last week that I thought Tyson Bagent’s film against the Jets was a little better than I expected it to be on second watch. Unfortunately, and this might be hard to believe, I think the Packers tape was worse than I thought it would be. I’m not sure if he lost confidence after the first pick and things unraveled from there, but it was truly awful tape. I’ve seen some criticism of Ben Johnson’s gameplay, and I’d just invite anyone with that opinion to make sure they watch the tape before settling into that as their final answer. Johnson was far from perfect, but he did more than enough schematically for Bagent to succeed. The biggest criticism you could have of Johnson was his decision to start Bagent over Keenum in the first place, which may be fair.

Bagent’s workout of the burpee broad jump mile made some waves a couple years ago, which is easily the most insane workout I’ve ever heard of and I can’t get over it. I was asked recently if I wanted to do a Hyrox race, which features a burpee broad jump station as part of the experience. For 80 meters. Still too far for me, I think.

The Bears will likely get Caleb Williams back this week against the Atlanta Falcons. That’s great news as Atlanta has a lot of firepower in their skill players and the Bears may need to win a shootout. They’re dealing with some quarterback injury issues as well and it would be a huge win if Chicago sees Tua Tagovailoa instead of Michael Penix. The fall between those two isn’t as big as Williams to Bagent, but it’s significant.

I watched that Atlanta – Baltimore game and it will be a good challenge for the Bears defense to try and limit Bijan Robinson in this one. Best defense against Bijan will likely be a Caleb Williams offense that runs out to an early lead and forces Atlanta into a negative game script. Forcing a banged-up Penix or a fully functioning Tua into throwing 35+ times will lead to turnover opportunities, something this Bears defense desperately needs.

This time last year I was in New Zealand. One of those once-in-a-lifetime trips. I always try to eat local fare wherever I travel and of course, I had my share of kiwifruit. I’ve kept that going back stateside but I’m a much bigger fan of the gold kiwifruit. Pro tip: cut the kiwifruit in half and scoop with a spoon.

I’m officially panicking about Jaylon Johnson. Problem is, the Bears don’t really have anywhere to go on that one. Kyler Gordon’s return only goes so far.

We’re officially on Khalil Mack watch, and I, for one, couldn’t be happier. He’s playing some good football on a bad Chargers squad and one would like to believe that Chicago would be the one place he’d be happy to go back to a place with familiarity and where he’s beloved. It’s a position of need for Chicago, and everything is lining up perfectly. I also personally love the idea of Mack returning so I can dig out that throwback jersey and wear it again.

You got any musings? Hit the comments and let me know what’s up.

item.title: 8 winners and 7 losers through the Bengals’ first 5 games of the 2026 NFL season
item.description: Here are’s a look at our Bengals winners and loses through the first five weeks of the season.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals are 3-2 heading into their Week 6 bye, and while there’s been plenty to get excited about, there’s also been plenty of cause for concern.

Despite their winning record, the Bengals are a far cry from the team we envisioned after their Week 2 victory in Houston. There have been some outstanding individual performances, but there have also been some glaring disappointments.

With five games in the books, it’s time to take stock of who’s exceeding expectations and who’s falling short.

Here are the Bengals’ winners and losers through the first five weeks of the season, starting with the good.

WINNERS

Evan McPherson

McPherson has absolutely earned the nickname “Money Mac” so far this season. He’s been perfect through five games, connecting on all 10 of his field-goal attempts, including a season-long 58-yarder. Incredibly, five of those 10 attempts have come from beyond 50 yards.

What’s even more impressive, though, is that McPherson hasn’t missed a field goal since Week 11 of the 2025 season. He’s now made 22 consecutive field goals, setting a new franchise record previously held by Shayne Graham.

Hopefully, he’ll continue adding to that total and establish a record that takes a generation to break.

Amarius Mims

Mims has been outstanding at right tackle for the Bengals this season. He’s currently ranked as PFF’s 10th-best offensive tackle with a pass-blocking grade of 78.8, having allowed just four total pressures and one sack.

His run-blocking grade leaves a little to be desired, but let’s face it: The Bengals’ offense is going to run through Joe Burrow and the passing game more often than not.

Mims’ ability to protect Burrow’s right side has been nothing short of fantastic, and he’s quickly establishing himself as one of the most important pieces of Cincinnati’s offensive line.

Boye Mafe

The Bengals appear to have struck gold in free agency at the edge rusher position once again.

Coming off a Super Bowl championship season with the Seattle Seahawks, Mafe signed a three-year deal with Cincinnati and has wasted no time making his presence felt.

He’s currently tied with Byron Young for the second-most quarterback hurries in the NFL with 20, just one behind league leader Aidan Hutchinson.

Mafe has also been solid against the run, earning a respectable 75.1 run-defense grade from PFF.

Like Trey Hendrickson before him, Mafe has hit the ground running in Cincinnati. If he keeps playing at this level, his signing could go down as one of the Bengals’ best offseason moves.

Mike Gesicki

Gesicki caught four touchdown passes over his first two seasons with the Bengals.

Through five games in 2026, he’s already matched that total.

It’s clear opposing defenses are doing everything they can to prevent Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins from beating them. That’s created opportunities for Gesicki, who has flourished in his role as a tight end/slot receiver hybrid specializing in finding open space.

With Burrow, Chase, Higgins, and Gesicki all under contract through the 2027 season, the Bengals have the makings of an offensive core that could do some serious damage in the postseason.

Of course, they have to get there first.

Dexter Lawrence

Lawrence has been worth every bit of the No. 10 overall pick the Bengals traded to acquire him.

It’s hard to imagine anyone Cincinnati could have selected with that pick making the kind of immediate impact Lawrence has had on this defense.

He’s currently PFF’s third-ranked interior defensive lineman with an overall defensive grade of 82.5. The two players ranked ahead of him have played only about two-thirds as many snaps as Lawrence.

He also has the third-most quarterback hurries among defensive tackles and is tied for fifth in sacks at the position.

Lawrence is massive, disruptive, and capable of changing an opposing offense’s game plan simply by lining up across from it.

He’s been everything the Bengals could have hoped for when they shipped a top-10 pick to the Giants.

Jonathan Allen

Allen was somewhat overlooked among the Bengals’ offseason acquisitions, largely because his arrival was overshadowed by the blockbuster trade for Lawrence.

However, he’s been nearly as impressive, particularly as a pass rusher.

Through five games, Allen has recorded 10 quarterback hurries, four hits and two sacks from the interior of the defensive line, complementing Lawrence’s three sacks.

In a conference featuring Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen, and a division with Lamar Jackson and Aaron Rodgers, the Bengals need all the pass rushers they can get.

Allen and Lawrence have given Cincinnati an interior pass rush that opposing offenses simply can’t afford to ignore.

Dalton Risner

Risner appears to have been the final piece of the puzzle for the Bengals’ offensive line.

He’s currently PFF’s eighth-ranked guard with an overall offensive grade of 81.7, including an 80.7 run-blocking grade and a 73.7 pass-blocking grade.

For an offense as pass-happy as Cincinnati’s, having an offensive line that can be trusted is enormous.

This is also the first season of Burrow’s career in which he’s had the same five starting offensive linemen in consecutive seasons. That continuity, combined with Risner’s strong play, has helped give the Bengals some much-needed stability up front.

Risner is scheduled to become a free agent after this season, and if he finishes the year the way he’s started it, he’s going to earn himself a nice new contract.

Hopefully, the Bengals are the ones who give it to him.

Tee Higgins

Chase is the Bengals’ No. 1 receiver and, in my opinion, the best wide receiver in the NFL.

That shouldn’t take anything away from how fantastic Higgins has been this season.

He’s currently PFF’s 10th-ranked wide receiver with an outstanding overall offensive grade of 90.0, and he’s on pace for more than 90 receptions and 1,400 receiving yards.

He only has one touchdown through five games, but he’s been Mr. Reliable whenever opposing defenses devote extra attention to keeping Chase away from Burrow.

Higgins would be the unquestioned No. 1 receiver on plenty of NFL teams. The Bengals are fortunate enough to have him as their No. 2.

LOSERS

Orlando Brown Jr.

While everything seems to be going right at right tackle, the same can’t be said for the other side of Cincinnati’s offensive line.

Brown has struggled mightily to start the season.

Among offensive tackles who have played at least 80% of their team’s snaps, Brown ranks as the seventh-worst pass blocker, according to PFF, with a grade of 62.2. He’s also surrendered three sacks and 12 total pressures.

Speed rushers, in particular, have given him fits. At times, he almost looks like he’s trying to get a head start before the snap just to avoid getting beaten around the edge, putting himself at risk of drawing false-start penalties.

Hopefully, the bye week gives Brown an opportunity to regroup and come back looking a little less stiff.

If his play doesn’t improve, though, finding Burrow a new blindside protector may need to become one of Cincinnati’s top priorities this offseason.

Darrin Simmons

Simmons has been the Bengals’ special teams coordinator since 2003 and their assistant head coach since 2020.

Usually, that’s a good thing. When special teams are doing their job, we rarely have much reason to talk about them.

Unfortunately, that’s not been the case this season.

Outside of McPherson’s outstanding kicking, Cincinnati’s special teams units have been unreliable, undisciplined and, at times, downright costly.

Against the Steelers, the Bengals committed a roughing-the-kicker penalty and muffed a punt, mistakes that ultimately resulted in 10 points for Pittsburgh.

The problems continued against Miami.

Lawrence was flagged for roughing the snapper, turning what would have been a Dolphins field goal into a touchdown. Erick All committed a 15-yard penalty that pushed McPherson out of field-goal range, and Dohnte Meyers fielded a kickoff near the four-yard line before allowing his momentum to carry him out of bounds.

That’s a lot of avoidable mistakes for a unit led by one of the longest-tenured special teams coordinators in the league.

Simmons needs his guys to come out of the bye week with renewed focus and discipline. The Bengals can’t afford to keep giving away points and field position.

Andrei Iosivas

Iosivas finds himself on this list through no real fault of his own.

Unfortunately, injuries don’t care about fairness.

Iosivas tore a ligament in his thumb, requiring surgery that could sideline him for four to six weeks. While that shouldn’t cost him the entire season, it has opened the door for Dohnte Meyers to stake his claim to the WR3 position.

Meyers is shifty in space, has shown value as a return specialist and has an awesome story to boot.

If he continues to make plays while Iosivas is sidelined, the Bengals could have a difficult decision to make when their veteran receiver is ready to return.

Iosivas may find himself fighting for the playing time that was his before the injury.

Jordan Battle

One good game doesn’t erase a bunch of bad ones.

Battle looked much better against the Dolphins, intercepting two passes, one of which was tipped, and showing significant improvement as a tackler.

Unfortunately, that performance came after a rough opening stretch.

Before the Miami game, Battle had already missed seven tackles, according to PFF, tying him for the fourth-most in the NFL.

The Bengals added Bryan Cook and Kyle Dugger this offseason, but they still need Battle to step up as a veteran safety familiar with the system.

Outside of his strong showing in Miami, he hasn’t done nearly enough.

Hopefully, that game was the beginning of a turnaround rather than an outlier.

Zac Taylor

Yes, the Bengals started 2-0.

Yes, they have a winning record heading into the bye.

And yes, things look pretty good on paper.

But we’re still seeing some of the same old Zac Taylor-isms that have frustrated Bengals fans for years.

Despite a renewed commitment to the running game and an effort to get Burrow under center more often, Cincinnati still hasn’t figured out how to run the football consistently.

Taylor’s offensive play-calling has lacked imagination even when things are going well. When the offense struggles, that lack of creativity becomes even more glaring.

And Taylor isn’t just the offensive play-caller. He’s the head coach. He’s steering the whole ship.

The defense has been inconsistent, special teams have committed costly mistakes, and the offense hasn’t always looked like the well-oiled machine it should be with Burrow, Chase and Higgins leading the way.

At the end of the day, the buck stops with Taylor.

He’s got some serious kinks to iron out during the bye week, because a 3-2 record isn’t going to mean much if the same problems keep showing up.

Bryan Cook

Cook was arguably the Bengals’ most significant addition to the secondary this offseason.

The front office elected not to sign any cornerbacks, instead investing in two safeties, including Cook, who was considered the top safety available in free agency.

Unfortunately, the early returns haven’t been encouraging.

Cook has already missed a game and a half through Cincinnati’s first five contests, and according to PFF, he’s on pace for one of the worst seasons of his career.

He’s currently posting career-low marks in run defense and overall defensive grade, along with the second-worst coverage grade of his career. He’s also on pace to match his career high in missed tackles.

To be fair, Cook is learning a new defensive system, and that adjustment can take time.

However, the Bengals didn’t bring him in to be a developmental project. They signed him to be a difference-maker in a secondary that desperately needed help.

Cincinnati needs the version of Cook who helped the Chiefs win championships to show up on the other side of the bye week.

The running game

Remember all that talk about establishing the run this offseason?

Well, we’re five games into the season, and it’s still mostly just talk.

The Bengals made a concerted effort to balance their offense, putting Burrow under center more frequently than they had through the first five weeks of any previous season.

The idea was simple: Make the offense less predictable, take some pressure off Burrow and force defenses to respect the running game.

So far, it hasn’t worked.

The Bengals’ longest run of the season is just 13 yards, the shortest in the NFL. They’re also averaging a miserable 3.6 yards per carry, tied for the fourth-worst mark in the league. That’s not just a lack of explosive plays. That’s an inability to consistently move the ball on the ground.

The Bengals have one of the most talented passing attacks in football, but they can’t expect Burrow to carry the entire offense every single week. At some point, Cincinnati has to figure out how to run the ball.

item.title: Checking in on former Detroit Lions players lost this offseason
item.description: Checking in on Detroit Lions free agent losses and how they’re doing on their new team.
item.content:encoded:
This offseason, the Detroit Lions made an unusual number of changes to their roster. With a tightening salary cap and a need to get younger, the Lions said goodbye to several players who had long been part of the organization.

With the Lions on their bye week, we thought this would be a good chance to check in on those departed players and see how they’re doing with their new teams.

RB David Montgomery

New team: Texans
Stats: 52 carries, 138 yards (2.7 YPC), 2 TDs; 7 catches, 67 yards, 1 TD
PFF grade: 68.1 (20th out of 53)

Montgomery is getting a bigger share of carries than he would’ve in Detroit (Woody Marks has 11 more carries than Montgomery at 149), but the efficiency numbers have fallen off a cliff. Montgomery’s 2.7 yards per carry is the lowest of his career by a full yard, and his 40.4% rushing success rate is also a career-low.

Unfortunately, Montgomery suffered a groin injury last week and is considered week-to-week.

WR Kalif Raymond

New team: Bears
Stats: 24 catches, 226 yards, 1 TD; 9 punt returns, 93 yards (10.3 avg.)
PFF grade: 73.0 (34th out of 97)

Raymond is already close to surpassing his yardage total from last year with the Lions (289) and is on pace for a career year. He has played in 62.4% of the Bears’ offensive snaps, which is his highest percentage since his first year in Detroit (71.4%). But his production has slowed down, catching five passes for 12 total yards in the last two games combined—albeit with a pair of backup quarterbacks.

WR Greg Dortch

New team: Bills
Stats: 0 catches; 9 punt returns, 84 yards (9.3 avg.); 16 kick returns, 421 yards (26.3 avg.)
PFF grade: 72.1 return grade (12th out of 70th)

Dortch has only played in 11 snaps on offense, but he’s been a solid returner for the Bills—something the Lions could certainly use after the injury to Tom Kennedy. Dortch’s punt return average is below league average, but his kick return average is just above it.

G Kayode Awosika

New team: Chargers
Stats: 2 starts
PFF grade: 59.2 (44th out of 81)

Awosika won the starting left guard job for the Chargers out of training camp, but has missed the last three games with a fibula injury. For what it’s worth, he’s currently graded higher than Lions’ reserve guard Ben Bartch (48.0).

DT Roy Lopez

New team: Cardinals
Stats: 5 starts — 20 tackles, 1.0 sacks, 3 TFLs
PFF grade: 71.3 (21st out of 140)

As Lions fans saw a taste of on Sunday, Lopez continues to play strong football on the interior. He’s been a big reason why the Cardinals have a strong run defense, and he flashed some of his pass-rushing chops with his first sack of the season opposite Juice Scruggs.

DT DJ Reader

New team: Giants
Stats: 5 starts—13 tackles
PFF grade: 85.8 (2nd out of 140)

Reader apparently still has it at age 32. He’s not only continued to be a strong run defender (77.4, fourth), but PFF is giving him an outstanding pass-rushing grade at 78.5 (eighth) despite producing only five pressures this year.

Also interesting, despite having Reader playing at his best, the Giants run defense is giving up the second-highest yards per carry average (5.2) in the NFL.

EDGE Al-Quadin Muhammad

New team: Buccaneers
Stats: 5 games, 2 starts — 4 tackles, 2 QB hits, 0.0 sacks
PFF grade: 77.1 (24th out of 123)

Muhammad’s standard stat sheet is quite bare, as he continues to look for his first sack of the season and only has four pressures through five games. However, PFF credits him with above-average scores in every phase of the game.

EDGE Marcus Davenport

New team: Bears (now retired)
Stats: 1 game — 1 tackle
PFF grade: 70.8

I felt compelled to add Davenport to this list, given he was considered a starter in Detroit. He made the Bears’ practice squad, got an elevation for a game, and announced his retirement from football last week.

EDGE Tyrus Wheat

New team: Cowboys
Stats: 4 games — 3 tackles (14 defensive snaps, 67 special teams snaps)
PFF grade: 61.9 PFF special teams grade

After logging 215 special teams snaps for the Lions last year, Wheat remains a staple on the third phase of the game in Dallas.

LB Alex Anzalone

New team: Buccaneers
Stats: 5 starts — 27 tackles, 1.0 sacks, 1 INT
PFF grade: 41.1 (75 out of 76)

Anzalone’s start to his Tampa career was a complete disaster, with fans callingfor his benching after just two games. He’s since settled in a bit, and he helped the Bucs get their first win of the season on Thursday with a game-clinching interception. What has been particularly concerning about his play is missed tackles. He had four in the first two games of the season after tallying just eight all of last year.

LB Grant Stuard

New team: Rams
Stats: 5 games — 2 tackles (0 defensive snaps, 99 special teams snaps)
PFF grade: 66.9 special teams grade

Stuard remains a four-core special teamer with the Rams, but has yet to find the field on defense.

CB Amik Robertson

New team: Commanders
Stats: 5 starts — 33 tackles, 8 passes defended, 1 forced fumble
PFF grade: 74.9 (13th out of 111)

If there’s one player the Lions may regret letting go, it’s Robertson—who signed a lucrative two-year, $15 million contract with Washington this offseason. Robertson has been excellent, leading the league with eight passes defended. He’s allowed a passer rating of just 79.8 when targeted (17 catches on 31 targets for 158 yards and 1 TD). However, he does have five penalties on the season—second-most among all cornerbacks.

He remains an elite run defender, producing an 87.3 grade in that phase —fifth-best among all cornerbacks.

S Daniel Thomas

New team: Browns
Stats: 3 games (0 starts) — 4 tackles (0 defensive snaps, 64 special teams snaps)
PFF grade: 69.8 special teams grade

The Lions didn’t have room for Thomas after overhauling the safety room, but he’s been an effective special teamer in Cleveland

  • TE Shane Zylstra (unsigned)
  • OT Taylor Decker (unsigned)
  • C Graham Glasgow (unsigned)
  • EDGE Josh Paschal (unsigned)
  • LB Zach Cunningham (unsigned)

item.title: Cowboys news: Dallas has made some changes to the defensive structure
item.description: Here is today’s Dallas Cowboys news
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys promised changes after the Tampa Bay Bucs game, and on the defensive side of the ball they are delivering change. Christian Parker got help and is moving his game day operation.

The team has also been bitten by the injury bug just six weeks into the NFL season. With 12 games remaining, the Cowboys have to be mindful of their remaining designated-to-return spots if anyone else is expected to miss a long period of time.

Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker making big change ahead of Week 6 – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram

Coming off a mini-bye week, Christian Parker is changing his game-day routine.

Part of the solution-based conversations over the weekend within the coaching staff included hiring longtime NFL defensive coordinator Mike Pettine as a senior adviser to defensive coordinator Christian Parker. Another part, as told by owner Jerry Jones on 105.3 The Fan on Tuesday morning, will be Parker moving from the sideline to the coaches’ booth beginning this week.

“You search for what we could do differently that would give us different results,” Jones said. “That’s the main emphasis that we would spend some specific attention to. We’re going to coach the defense, from not on the field, but up above. Parker is going up above. You should be looking for ways to improve.”

Cowboys have a specific IR issue that threatens 2026 – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com

Christian Parker’s side of the ball has taken the biggest hit from injuries.

The current problem for the Cowboys is that they’ve only played five games but have already used six of their eight allotted IR-DTR seats.

The league caps the usage of them at two during final roster cutdowns, and Marist Liufau and rookie cornerback Devin Moore were moved into them ahead of the season. The subsequent additions have included All-Pro guard Tyler Smith (who has since returned to action), Jalen Thompson, P.J. Locke and Jonathan Bullard.
