item.title: Broncos vs. Seahawks: 3 Players to Watch in Week 6
item.description: In order for the Denver Broncos to defeat the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football, these three players have to perform well.
item.content:encoded:
The stakes are high when the Denver Broncos host the Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football. Finding a way to topple the defending Super Bowl champions is going to be extremely difficult. Here are three players that need to perform at a high level in order for Denver to earn their fourth victory of the season.

Riley Moss — Cornerback

On a short week, it’s still uncertain if Riley Moss is going to play on Thursday Night Football. He has been limited in Denver’s practice sessions thus far. We will probably know much more sometime this afternoon in that respect. In the event he doesn’t, you can just throw in “Whoever is tasked with covering Jaxon Smith-Njigba”here instead.

The Broncos have faced some really good offenses to start the season. In my mind, there is no doubt Smith-Njigba is the premier playmaker for the Seahawks on offense. He is the reigning Offensive Player of the Year. The star wide receiver already has four 100 receiving yard performances this season, seven touchdowns, and is on pace to shatter the career best numbers he put up last in 2025.

Denver’s banged up secondary will be without Patrick Surtain II and Talanoa Hufanga. That will make it even harder to limit Smith-Njigba’s impact. If Moss is a go, I expect most of that responsibility to be on his shoulders.

The savvy wideout can beat you deep and he can create after the catch. He’s one of the most well-rounded receivers in the NFL. I’m very interested to see what kind of coverage plan Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph has in store to keep him from having a huge game.

Jaylen Waddle — Wide Receiver

The Broncos traded multiple premium picks to add Jaylen Waddle to their receiving corps. The hope was that the sixth-year wideout would be an impact player for the team and take their passing attack to new heights. Unfortunately, Waddle has been missing in action for most of the season.

Outside of the Broncos’ Week 2 win versus the Jacksonville Jaguars where he had eight catches for 138 yards, the sixth-year wideout hasn’t made much of an impact. He has just 18 catches for 204 yards and 1 touchdown. Through five games, Waddle is sporting the worst catch percentage of his career at 58-percent.

The Seahawks have been phenomenal shutting down opposing team’s passing attacks. Even so, this is a game where Waddle has to make an impact for the Broncos. They invested a lot of resources to acquire him, and the early returns aren’t too great. Can he rebound and be a difference maker in primetime? Denver will need that to happen to be victorious.

Bo Nix — Quarterback

It’s been a slow start to Bo Nix’s third season as the starting quarterback of the Broncos. I’m quite honestly surprised. I felt he was poised for a big jump in productivity and efficiency. Unfortunately, the results thus far aren’t great.

In four of five games, Nix has thrown for less than 215 yards. Four of those contests have resulted in a completion percentage below at or below 60-percent. He has also had a turnover in four of five games. He has one of the worst EPA ranking for any quarterback in the NFL.

The Seahawks sport a very good defense. They force turnovers, are fantastic on third down, and are allowing just 150 yards per game through the air. This will be a very tough game for Nix to get back on track. However, the Broncos desperately need a spark and much better play from their third-year signal caller.

Can he hit some concepts over the middle of the field? Will he be able to find a few big plays down the field like he did often during the ’25 season? I have no idea if that transpires. If it does, I really like Denver’s chances of winning. Most importantly, I also think a good performance would give him a much-needed boost of confidence. I don’t expect an elite performance, but I want to see a good outing from Bo on Thursday Night Football.

item.title: 5 Giants-Saints storylines: Optimism in the midst of ‘crazy town’
item.description: Giants “right in the middle of it,” and sense an opportunity.
item.content:encoded:
“A pessimist sees the difficulty in every opportunity; an optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty.”

New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh is a Winston Churchill admirer. In trying to make a point during his Monday call with New York media, Harbaugh was reaching to recall that Churchill quote as the coach was describing the positive attitude of quarterback Jameis Winston.

Here is the full quote from Harbaugh about Winston:

“It’s awesome. I mean, it’s how important is it for a person? I mean, it’s the best thing to be around, and it’s genuine. I mean, he’s a very strong faith person. He’s a very strong Christian. He is a very good guy. He works extremely hard. He’s very motivated. He’s an unbelievable competitor. He’s tough as can be. He’s a fighter, and he just doesn’t let adversity get him down. He understands. It’s like (former NBA player) Michael Jordan or (16th President of the United States) Abraham Lincoln or all the different stories you’ve heard. It’s not how many times you get knocked down, it’s how many times you get back up. You need to be plus-one in the get up category. And that’s exactly what he does every single day of his life, I would say.

“And that’s why people like him are always successful. I mean, most successful people are optimists. Didn’t (former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Winston) Churchill say that he knew a lot of successful people in his life. He knew a lot of pessimists in his life. And none of the successful people were the pessimists. Are you aware of that quote? It’s along those lines.”

Why do I bring this up? Because Harbaugh, Winston and the Giants are trying each week to be the optimists in a difficult situation.

They have lost their quarterback, Jaxson Dart, for the season. Yet, they have gone 2-0-1 since. They have lost their defensive leader, Brian Burns, for the season. Yet, players like Abdul Carter, Arvell Reese, Jevon Holland and Tae Banks have stepped up to help the Giants go without a loss in their last three games.

Some want to belittle the NFC East, throwing around the ‘NFC Least’ moniker with the long-downtrodden Giants leading the division while the Philadelphia Eagles and Dallas Cowboys lose winnable games, and the Washington Commanders embarrass themselves.

The Giants, though, are trying to play the role of the optimistic opportunist in the midst of the NFC East chaos. The Giants have commissioned ‘1-0’ t-shirts you often see Harbaugh and the players wearing. The idea, of course, is to just focus on going 1-0 every week despite the chaos of the division, the players who aren’t and won’t be there to help, and even the daily disruption of the construction at the Giants’ facility that has players lockering, showering, and lifting in temporary quarters in a parking lot once reserved for staff and media.

In the middle of ‘crazy-town’

Even Sunday against the Commanders, the pessimist would say the Giants should have won the game. And, certainly there is an argument to be made for that. The optimist would say despite everything that happened in overtime they were down 14 points with eight minutes to play and did not lose. And they gained ground in the division despite the game ending in a tie.

“We just got to really just do the best we can. Because you just can’t predict what’s going to happen,” Harbaugh said. “And you’ve got to keep chasing all those things all the time, every week. You got to keep rolling through. You can’t practice them all in one week. So, you got to keep rolling through them as much as you can. Don’t get complacent. Look for new things. If you see something, if you see a hole in what you’re doing, try to plug it up before it comes up. But man, it’s a crazy league. My wife, she was visiting my daughter and so I was talking to her after the game. And she’s watching games on TV. And she says, the whole NFL is like crazy-town right now. It’s crazy-town. It’s like, there’s so much crazy going on in this league right now. That’s what makes it so exciting, I guess.

“And we were right in the middle of it. And we would like to do a lot of things better, we’d like to play. And we’re so proud of the good things and things we did well. And there’s so many things that we know we can do better. And we’re going to chase, we’re going to chase with everything we’ve got. Because we’ve got next week to try to be a better football team. And our guys are very, very optimistic. They’re very optimistic about that. Very optimistic that they can improve and get better and get ready for the next challenge.”

The Rodney Dangerfield of the NFL

This one goes along with the ‘NFC Least’ theme. The Giants are in sole possession first place in the NFC East five games into the season. The New Orleans Saints, the Giants’ Week 6 opponent, are 1-4. The game will be at MetLife Stadium, where the Giants are 3-0 this season.

Despite that, FanDuel Sportsbook has installed the Saints as 1.5-point favorites.

I get that the combined record of New Orleans’ opponents is 17-8 (.680 winning percentage), while Giants’ opponents are 6-18-1 (.260 winning percentage).

Yes, the Saints are likely better than their record and may still make a run at a title in the less-than-spectacular NFC South. Still, the Giants being the home underdog in this situation feels disrespectful.

Running the ball

The Giants are built to be a running team. They are 29th in the NFL in their usage of ‘11’ personnel, a more wide open offensive set with one running back, one tight end, and three wide receivers. They are first in the league in their usage of ‘22’ personnel, which is two running backs, two tight ends, one wide receiver. Patrick Ricard has played 116 snaps, more than any other fullback in the league.

The Giants want to play power football with Ricard, blocking tight end Chris Manhertz, and straight-ahead pile-pushing backs Cam Skattebo and Najee Harris.

Unfortunately, the complement to all of that — Jaxson Dart’s ability to create chunk plays in the quarterback run game — is gone for the remainder of the season.

The Giants tried on Sunday against the Commanders to reinsert the threat of that quarterback run game by using J.J. McCarthy for a few plays. It didn’t work, but Harbaugh won’t give up on it after just one try.

The Giants know they have to do something. The numbers are not pretty:

  • They still do not have a 20-yard run from a running back this season — Skattebo’s overtime 19-yarder in Week 5 is their longest.
  • Only eight teams have fewer than the Giants’ 10 runs of at least 10 yards.
  • The Giants’ EPA per rush is -0.15, 26th in the league.
  • The Giants average 3.7 yards per running play, 24th overall.
  • Their rushing success tate of 38.8% is 21st.
  • The Giants have -65 rushing yards over expected, meaning NextGen Stats believes their rushers have left at least 65 yards on the table. That’s 29th.
  • The Giants are 26th in the league in yards before contact (0.86).
  • Defenses are nullifying the Giants’ run game without stacking the box with extra defenders. The Giants have faced a stacked box just 19% of the time, 24th in the NFL.

“We definitely need more explosives in the run game,” Harbaugh said on Monday. “That’s definitely something that we’ll be chasing and looking for. Every play has got its own story that is told. We look back at it and study it. I think everybody in the offense will tell you this play, that play, whatever. There’s always something that can be done better. A lot of times it’s the difference in the play. It’s really our execution mostly, usually. Sometimes you’re overwhelmed with numbers or something like that. But there’s definitely been plays where we can get more yards on.

“We’ve got all the players we need to win all the games, to win every single game. All the players we need to win every single game. But we’re always looking too, to get better. The first way to get better is that the players, you have get better. That’s really what you focus on. Focus on your guys improving every single day at what we do. We’ll get better at the run game because we’re going to run the ball and we’re going to practice running the ball.

This is what Harbaugh told Big Blue View about the run game before the Week 5 contest against Washington:

“We’re just not good enough yet. Defenses are playing us pretty well. As we get better, we’ll probably have more longer runs. Also, if we make them pay a little more with play action, I think that’ll loosen them up a little bit, probably. But we just got to keep getting better. I think the guys are working hard at it. We’re playing very hard. We’re trying to play very physically. So, all the elements are there. We just have to get better, keep getting better.”

They did not accomplish getting better against the Commanders. How can they do that going forward? This week, specifically?

The view here is that the Giants need to become less predictable. BBV’s Chris Pflum looked at the predictability of the run game and offered some potential fixes earlier in the week.

Here are some thoughts of my own:

  • More snaps and touches for Tyrone Tracy. He is the most versatile back the Giants have, and the back most likely to make someone miss in the open field.
  • Spreading the field more with fewer heavy sets. Or, at least breaking some tendencies they have shown based on formation. It is fairly easy to read the intent of the Giants’ offense based upon who is in the game.

The Giants may have stumbled upon part of the solution during their second half and overtime Sunday against Washington, when they leaned into more tempo and were less run-heavy. Jameis Winston dropped back 60 times against Washington, throwing 54 passes. That’s too many, but being a bit less 1940s ‘3 yards and a cloud of dust’ reliant is likely a good idea.

“It [the tempo] was good, no question. We’ve been talking about some of the tempo stuff. We’ve been working on that. It’s been part of our system from Day 1, really. It’s something we built in from the beginning,” Harbaugh said on Monday. “And it was good to get to it. We’ve been talking about getting to it.

“We got to it maybe because we had to. Maybe you’re right. Maybe game flow forced us to do it, but it was a good thing in that sense. So yeah, it opened up the offense. It was good to see, and it probably needs to be part of what we’re doing going forward.”

We will see if the Giants, continuing to evolve on offense with Winston at the controls rather than Dart, begin to operate a bit differently this Sunday. Results to date indicate that, as important as running the ball well is, the Giants are going to have to loosen things up a bit in order to get that done.

‘Feast or famine’ run defense

The Giants’ defense has not been horible against the run. Except for the reality that when the run defense has broken down it has REALLY broken down.

The Giants have given up six runs of 20 yards or more this season. Only three teams have surrendered more. And, granted, two of those runs were Sunday by Washington Commanders’ quarterback Jayden Daniels. But, they count. And both went for long touchdowns.

As a result of those long runs, the often solid run defense is still allowing an unacceptable 5.2 yards per carry, 31st in the NFL.

“I think we’ve had too many chunk plays overall. We’ve played kind of feast or famine run defense,” Harbaugh said on Monday. “We’ve had a lot of really good plays, a lot of really good plays in that game where we stuffed the run, which we’re very capable of doing. And then there’s a couple of line of scrimmage runs that get out on us that we’re not happy about that can be played so much better. Whether we don’t adjust to a motion the right way, we don’t get over in our gaps, we don’t quite come in through the angles. I think sometimes our tackling in the back end is really good. And sometimes it’s not good, especially if it’s spacey.”

Daniels ran for scores of 38 and 26 yards for Washington on Sunday. While no other quarterback in the NFL is as dangerous running the ball, Harbaugh was not happy with how the Giants defended those plays.

“Those were plays that should not have gotten out,” Harbaugh said. “We did not play those right with our rush lanes. We know that, everybody knows it. And it hadn’t been a problem the last couple weeks, really. It was a problem the first week, and we got to make it not a problem next week.”

Tyler Shough of the Saints has mobility, but not nearly in the way Daniels does.

The other problem for the Giants is finding defensive tackle depth behind D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris. Both veterans have played well. You can’t live with a two-man defensive line rotation, though, and beyond those two the Giants have struggled.

Chauncey Golston is on IR. Second-year man Darius Alexander is playing more, but his run defense remains inconsistent. C.J. Okoye was displaced on a 33-yard touchdown run by Jacory Croskey-Merritt on Sunday, and is only playing about 15 snaps per game.

Rookie Bobby Jamison-Travis has been inactive for all five games. The Giants have veterans Josh Tupou, P.J. Mustipher, C.J. Ravenall, and Dawuane Smoot on their practice squad.

Could any of those players help the rotation?

Offensive line injuries

Right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor might not play against the Saints after suffering a calf injury in Week 5, Harbaugh listed Eluemunor, Colton Hood (concussion), and Tyler Nubin (neck) as “day-to-day.”

Eluemunor had to be helped off the field Sunday against the Commanders. He had an MRI Monday. Let’s see how much he practices this week.

Marcus Mbow will start at right tackle with rookie J.C. Davis as the swing tackle if Eluemunor can’t play.

The other injury concern is left tackle Andrew Thomas. He has been fighting through a Week 2 groin injury that has limited his ability to practice. He has not missed any game time, but it’s not hard to see that he isn’t at his best.

“I think he’s doing a really good job of just playing through whatever he’s got. I mean, guys have things this time of year. He’s doing a great job. He’s so tough. Got the Purple Heart (a weekly award the Giants give out for displaying toughness) last week,” Harbaugh said. “He’s playing at a high level. I mean, it may be laboring for him, but still the result is better than almost every player in the league at that position.”

item.title: Not just Big Q: Colts have another standout offensive guard playing some elite ball
item.description: The Colts may have one of the league’s best kept secrets at starting right guard, right now.
item.content:encoded:
We’re always searching for silver linings as the Indianapolis Colts sit at 2-3, but look closer to approaching a full blown rebuild than realistically contending for a Super Bowl title anytime soon.

One of them is regarding the standout play so far of starting offensive lineman Matt Goncalves, the 3rd-year pro who just began his second season as a full-time starter at right guard due to positional necessity.

The former 2024 Colts’ 3rd round pick out of Pitt is blossoming into one of the better young starting offensive guards in all of football right before our very own eyes this 2026 season.

While there was consensus concern among Colts fans that allowing breakout starting right guard Will Fries, who Indianapolis will face in two weeks, to leave in free agency to the Minnesota Vikings in the 2025 offseason, would prove to be a critical mistake in hindsight, Goncalves appears to have sufficiently filled those rather large shoes.

Per PFF, Goncalves is their 12th best graded offensive guard with a +75.9 overall grade through 5 starts in the 2026 campaign. Specifically, he’s allowed just a sack and 3 total QB pressures so far in 195 total pass blocking snaps. His allowed pass pressure rate (5.7%) is among the best at his starting right guard position.

If this keeps up, the big man, approaching 320 pounds, can chug as many footballs as he wants in celebration!

item.title: Ravens news: Jesse Minter cracked the NFL’s new overtime rules
item.description: Rounding up the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover the praise for Jesse Minter’s overtime strategy on Sunday night against the Falcons, Tyler Loop flashing his range, and an update on just how good Zay Flowers is this year.

Did the Ravens reinvent NFL overtime?

When Kyle Hamilton won the overtime coin toss, most expected him to announce that the Ravens were kicking off. Conventional wisdom regarding the league’s new(ish) overtime rules dictated that teams wanted to possess the ball second so they had an information advantage. Depending on the results of the first drive, they would know exactly how many points they need to score to win or keep the game going.

The Ravens had other plans. Head coach Jesse Minter – aided by game management coordinator Charlie Gelman and others on the staff – wanted to take advantage of a tired Falcons defense that just let Tyler Huntley drive down the field in less than two minutes. Atlanta’s vaunted run defense did not hold up against Derrick Henry and Justice Hill, and Huntley had (finally) settled into a rhythm through the air.

Baltimore’s defense had also just injured Falcons quarterback Michael Penix on the final drive of regulation. He said after the game that he could have taken the field if Atlanta got the ball first. But Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle executed a masterful 14-play drive that took 7 minutes (and three seconds) off the clock. In that time, the adrenaline keeping Penix’s pain at bay subsided. He threw on the sidelines, but Tua Tagovailoa instead entered the game. Kyle Hamilton took care of things from there.

Not every team is as capable of executing a clock-killing drive as one with Henry in the backfield. It would be interesting to see Lamar Jackson under center in these scenarios; it’s almost hard for him (and Zay Flowers) to not generate explosive plays. Other NFL teams will still try to copycat the Ravens’ success on Sunday night in future overtime games, which could also put the league in position for more ties.

The Ravens hacked NFL overtime to beat the Falcons – James Dator (SB Nation)

Using a heavy dose of Derrick Henry and short passing from Tyler Huntley, the Ravens executed a 14-play, 7:03-minute touchdown drive that both moved the ball all the way down the field for a touchdown, but critically forced the Falcons to use both of their timeouts, while leaving fewer than 3 minutes left on the clock.

Henry ran the ball six times on the drive, the longest pass completion was for 10 yards. So much time was taken off the clock that when Baltimore was at 2nd and goal it was almost as if the Falcons had to the let them score, just to ensure they had a chance to possess the ball.

Ben Gretch (Stealing Signals)

What happened last night is the Falcons had to use both of their overtime timeouts on defense to preserve time. They got the ball back with just under three minutes, and only the 2-minute stoppage, and it forced them to be one-dimensional.

On the broadcast, Collinsworth suggested kicking to force the Atlanta QB situation onto the field quicker. What Baltimore did attacked the Atlanta QB situation more; if Atlanta got ball first, they could’ve tried a run-based offense. They really couldn’t do that with 2:50 and no timeouts.

Setting aside the specifics of Atlanta’s QB situation, EPA models look at next-drive success, because that’s crucial in football. What I’m suggesting is missed here is when a team executes like Baltimore did last night, the opponent’s drive success takes a substantial hit because of the clock constraint…

…Anyway, Baltimore executed this brilliantly last night, and more teams should take note. Kicking off gives your opponent the ability to execute this. The Falcons didn’t necessarily run well last night, but they’ve been great on the ground in other recent games, and an alternate result last night where they had ball first could’ve been them executing a run-based offense that bled clock and put the Ravens in the situation they found themselves in, with not enough time to run a balanced offense and force to be one-dimensional and throw.

Tyler Loop’s big leg is finally showing up

NFL Week 5: Big takeaways, questions and fantasy spin from Sunday’s games – Jamison Hensley (ESPN)

Trend to watch: Ravens kicker Tyler Loop has become automatic from long range. He hit two field goals from 51 yards, improving to 5-of-5 from 50 yards or longer this season. This is a major change from last season, when Loop was 1-of-4 from 50 or longer as a rookie.

Ravens news, notes and opinions: Reinforcements on the way, Year 2 growth and Tyler Loop’s range – Jeff Zrebiec (The Athletic)

Long-distance Loop

Tyler Loop made just one of four field-goal attempts from 50-plus yards last year. While Ravens coaches consistently touted his big leg, he faltered in his limited opportunities from distance.

Through five games this year, he’s 5-for-5 from 50-plus yards, and the Ravens don’t win the Cowboys or Falcons games without his ability to come through on long kicks.

Zay Flowers’ numbers through six weeks are (still) ridiculous

Zay Flowers Is Redefining What a No. 1 Wide Receiver Looks Like – Ryan Mink (BaltimoreRavens.com)

There shouldn’t have been any questions about Flowers’ premier status after he finished seventh in the NFL in receiving yards last season. But the same tired “Is he a No. 1?” question arose when the Ravens gave Flowers a four-year, reportedly $140 million contract extension this offseason, ranking him fourth in average annual salary among wide receivers.

Flowers has put the question to bed this season. By any metric, he’s been the most productive and unguardable wide receiver on a per-snap basis in the NFL.

Flowers’ 405 receiving yards this season ranks eighth in the NFL, but he’s missed two games’ worth of snaps due to a hamstring injury. His quarterback, Lamar Jackson, has also now missed a game and a half.

Per route run, Flowers leads the NFL with 4.5 yards. When Jackson has been under center, Flowers has averaged 9.1 yards per route run (and 5.3 yards per play).

item.title: NFL Secret Superstars, Week 6: Snoop Huntley, Elijah Ponder, and Jordan Battle are the AFC’s surprise standouts
item.description: Huntley’s flawless comeback, Ponder’s breakout game, and Battle’s two-pick performance headline Week 5’s under-the-radar standouts in the AFC.
item.content:encoded:
Superstars may lead the discussion when it comes to success in the NFL, but more often than not, it’s the guys you barely know who will make the plays needed when they’re needed. Such players can be underrated for all kinds of reasons. Perhaps they’re playing in a smaller market, and the media isn’t appropriately trumpeting their exploits. Maybe they’re hidden in a depth chart behind bigger names who may not be doing as much. Or, it’s always possible that a wayward coach hasn’t quite figured out that one guy needs elevation to bring better results to the team.

Whatever the reason, we at SB Nation always like to bring the underrated names to you with the offseason Hidden Gems and in-season Secret Superstars series. You can also catch up on the AFC and NFC Secret Superstars for the 2026 season right here.

Here are our AFC Secret Superstars for Week 5 of the 2026 regular season. And if you haven’t yet, download the new SB Nation app, so you can better read our stuff and join the conversation wherever you are!

(All advanced metrics courtesy of Next Gen Stats, Pro Football Focus, Sports Info Solutions, and Sumer Sports unless otherwise indicated).

Tyler “Snoop” Huntley, QB, Baltimore Ravens

Things did not look good at all for the Baltimore Ravens at a certain point on Sunday night. Lamar Jackson was out with a sprained left ankle, and though Tyler “Snoop” Huntley is rightly regarded as one of the NFL’s better backup quarterbacks, Huntley was doing his thing against an Atlanta Falcons defense that came into Sunday Night Football tied with the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Las Vegas Raiders for the fifth-lowest EPA per play allowed at -0.01.

In Baltimore’s first nine drives, Atlanta’s Shark Week defense created a pressure rate of 53.8%, and in those first nine drives, Huntley completed 13 of 21 passes for 121 yards, one touchdown, no interceptions, a passer rating of 93.6, and an EPA per play of -0.39.

Down 23-15 with 2:17 left in regulation and with first-and-20 at his own 19-yard line after a holding penalty on offensive lineman Emery Jones Jr., Huntley went off as few could have expected.

In the drive that tied the game at 23-23, and in the overtime drive that eventually won the game 30-23, Huntley completed all 11 passes he threw for 80 yards, another touchdown, no interceptions, a passer rating of 127.3, and an EPA per play of +0.72. Oh, and he also pushed his way into the end zone with 3:01 left in overtime for the winning touchdown. All the Ravens had to do then was to wait for Tua Tagovailoa to throw a soul-crushing interception, and Tagovailoa complied.

When it was all over, Huntley had become the only player in pro football history to go 10-for-10 or more with a passing touchdown and a rushing touchdown in the final two minutes of regulation plus overtime.

Ever.

“Snoop’ is just like one of the coolest dudes,” Ravens head coach Jesse Minter said. “He doesn’t really get rattled. He’s just always the same, and he keeps such a good demeanor about him, [and] keeps his composure. He said, ‘Hey man, all we’re going to do is try and go 1-0 this week.’ That’s what he told me right before the game. And he just did his job, and he did it at a high level. I told the guys last night, ‘There’s not a locker room in the NFL that has more confidence in their backup quarterback than our guys have in Snoop.’ So, he did a great job. He played really well, played with more and more confidence as the game went on and as the moments got bigger, which is really cool to see.” 

Defensive lineman Calais Campbell, who has seen just about everything in his 19-year career, agreed.

“I am very proud of [Huntley], man. We always rally behind him. We know what he can do. When he is locked in and playing his game, he could beat anybody. He could put points up on anybody. We put 30 points on the board on a really good defense tonight. It took overtime, but he just kept making the surgical throw in the crucial moment. [On] third-and-shorts [and] third-and-longs, [he] just kept making the throws, and [he] never flinched. Bad things happen, adversity happens, [but] it is football. [You] just line up and play the next play.

“Tyler Huntley, man, anytime he is in the game, I have confidence.” 

It’s incredibly valuable to have the right backup quarterback, and in Huntley — the seven-year veteran from Utah who has won all three games he’s pitched in relief for the Ravens over the last two seasons — Baltimore has just such a player.

Everybody in the building agrees, and everybody in the building is right.

Elijah Ponder, EDGE, New England Patriots

In five seasons with the Cal Poly Mustangs from 2020-2024, edge-rusher Elijah Ponder did his best to up his profile, totaling 25 sacks and 151 pressures in his collegiate career. But you know how it is with a lot of smaller-school guys — they get lost in the shuffle. Evidently, smaller schools don’t even exist anymore to the Big Brains over at College GameDay.

Okay, rant over. In any case, I wasn’t really familiar with Ponder’s game until I was talking to various members of the Patriots’ defense during Super Bowl week, and his name kept coming up. The undrafted free agent made an impression in a rookie season with four sacks and 24 pressures in 210 pass-rushing snaps, and he was evidently on the verge.

Well, the verge has arrived in Year 2. The 6’3”, 245-pound Ponder has five sacks and 18 pressures this season in just 125 pass-rushing snaps, and he’s coming off a two-sack, five-pressure game against the Las Vegas Raiders — a 45-17 thrashing for the Patriots.

“Yeah, for sure,” Ponder said last week when asked if his second-year growth is real (as if you couldn’t see it on the tape). “As an undrafted rookie, you go in not knowing what to expect. You want to be there, you want to make the team, you want to make sure you learn all the things you need to learn, and apply them on the field to the best of your ability. I was a lot more, at least for me, in my head [as a rookie].”

Ponder has the tools to remain among the most productive and disruptive edge defenders in the NFL, and the time to buy stock is now.

Jordan Battle, Safety, Cincinnati Bengals

Through his first three seasons and four games of his NFL career, 2023 third-round Bengals safety Jordan Battle allowed 62 catches on 90 targets for 901 yards, six touchdowns, seven interceptions, six pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 91.0. Not bad for the Alabama alum, but not exactly Top 10 among deep safeties. So, in the week leading up to Cincinnati’s Sunday game against the Miami Dolphins, it was interesting to see Battle go all forensic on the tells that Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis gives to enemy defenses.

“He has a little slight little tap before every throw though, so I feel like we could use that as a key to break on the ball,” Battle said. “He likes to tap the ball before he throws it, or he takes his hand off, and that gives the read [for] the break. He’s obviously dangerous with his feet. We know we’ve got to be alert for that. Third-and-longs, they will run quarterback draws, and in the passing game, he will extend plays. So we got to be good downfield. DBs are plastering, so we got to be alert for that. He will take chances. We just got to be on, be alert on guys where they line up.”

So, Battle had done his homework, and it paid off. In Cincinnati’s 31-24 win that brought them to 3-2 on the season, Battle was targeted once, allowing no catches, and two interceptions. We can forever debate whether or not Willis was giving anything away — Battle’s first interception was on a pass deflected by Boye Mafe — but whatever Battle was doing in the film room, it showed up at the right times.

“Just a scramble drill, and just seeing him look down the field, and I’m just trying to get in the area — get in the position to make a play,” Battle said of his second interception.

Battle wasn’t just about the picks in this game. He also got Willis for a near-sack (a zero-yard gain) when he came down from the deep third in the first quarter, and he hurried Willis in the fourth quarter — albeit on Willis’ three-yard touchdown pass to receiver Kevin Coleman Jr. with 7:19 remaining.

Overall, it was quite the complete game for the fourth-year man.

“Very good,” Battle said when asked how it felt. “Obviously, we’re back in the win column. That’s what we wanted to do coming to this week.”

The Bengals’ defense has been on the upswing this season, and Battle’s informed actions helped a ton on Sunday.

item.title: Cardinals bring in 8 players for tryouts
item.description: For the current roster, or for the database?
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals brought in eight players on Tuesday for tryouts. Most likely, these are simply to update GM Monti Ossenfort’s player database, just in case a player becomes injured.

One player in particular looks like he was brought in as a possible keeper either on the main roster or the practice squad: OG Jamaree Salyer.

RELATED: CARDINALS WORK OUT FOUR SAFETIES

The player list appears to have a purpose regarding positions with four receivers, a QB, and two linebackers.

Among the athlete list is QB Conner Bazelak (6’-3”, 225 pounds). He was a six-year senior due to the pandemic. He played for Missouri, Indiana, and finally Bowling Green for his final two years. He had 53 college starts and passed for 12,349 yards with 66 touchdowns against 39 interceptions. He went undrafted last year and was on the Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ practice squad, then was a final-day cut this year.

Salyer (6’-4”, 335 pounds) played in 47 games in four years at Georgia. He was a full-time starter his final two seasons and won a National Championship in 2021. The Los Angeles Chargers made him a sixth-round draft pick in 2022. Salyer has played in 64 NFL games with 40 starts with LA, then signed with the Miami Dolphins as a free agent this spring, but was a final cutdown in August. He could fill the void left by losing OG Matt Pryor.

The other players who worked out include LBs Bradyn Swinson and Riley Wilson. The four receivers are Joaquin Davis, Courtney Jackson, Shedrick Jackson, and Dayton Wade.

Swinson (6’-4”, 255 pounds) of Oregon and LSU was a fifth-round pick of the New England Patriots in 2025 and played mainly on special teams. Wilson (6’-1”, 226 pounds) went undrafted out of Arizona this year and signed with the Patriots, was released, signed to the practice squad, then waived on September 29.

item.title: NFL Secret Superstars 2026: Bucky Irving, Christian Watson, and Renardo Green are Week 5’s NFC standouts
item.description: Irving’s 165-yard night, Watson’s two deep touchdowns against Chicago, and Green’s two picks of Sam Darnold headline the NFC’s under-the-radar standouts.
item.content:encoded:
Superstars may lead the discussion when it comes to success in the NFL, but more often than not, it’s the guys you barely know who will make the plays needed when they’re needed. Such players can be underrated for all kinds of reasons. Perhaps they’re playing in a smaller market, and the media isn’t appropriately trumpeting their exploits. Maybe they’re hidden in a depth chart behind bigger names who may not be doing as much. Or, it’s always possible that a wayward coach hasn’t quite figured out that one guy needs elevation to bring better results to the team.

Whatever the reason, we at SB Nation always like to bring the underrated names to you with the offseason Hidden Gems and in-season Secret Superstars series. You can also catch up on the AFC and NFC Secret Superstars for the 2026 season right here.

Here are our NFC Secret Superstars for Week 5 of the 2026 regular season. And if you haven’t yet, download the new SB Nation app, so you can better read our stuff and join the conversation wherever you are!

(All advanced metrics courtesy of Next Gen Stats, Pro Football Focus, Sports Info Solutions, and Sumer Sports unless otherwise indicated).

Bucky Irving, RB, Tampa Bay Buccaneers

“If you have a career day against the NFL’s worst defense?“ could be seen as football’s version of ”If a tree falls in the forest and nobody hears it, does it make a sound?“ Yes, the falling tree makes a sound regardless, but what does it all mean, man?

In the case of Tampa Bay Buccaneers third-year running back Bucky Irving, it means a lot. In the Buccaneers’ 24-16 Thursday night win over the Dallas Cowboys and their league-worst defense, the fourth-round man from Oregon by way of Minnesota had the game of his life. Irving ran the ball 21 times for 165 yards (7.86 yards per carry), with 120 yards after contact (5.71 per attempt), and he forced 11 missed tackles.

The 2026 Cowboys came into that game allowing 4.77 yards per carry, and 2.87 yards after contact per carry. That’s not completely awful, and it’s mostly because teams just want to tee off on the pass defense instead — and for good reason. But as the Bucs were starting undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels in relief of the injured Baker Mayfield, a comprehensive run game certainly would help, and that’s what the Buccaneers got.

Not that the Buccaneers had enjoyed a comprehensive run game in the first month of the season. Irving had run the ball 56 times for 241 yards, one touchdown, and 11 forced missed tackles in the opening four weeks, and Kenneth Gainwell had been even less exceptional, with 26 yards on 13 carries.

So, was this a breakout or an anomaly? Yes, the tape shows all kinds of run fit breakdowns and tackling nightmares, but on Irving’s 72-yard run at the start of the third quarter, tight end Cade Otton bumped into right guard Cody Mauch, nobody seemed to know who to block inside, and it was Irving who had to make the magic happen. Remember: It’s not as if the Buccaneers’ offense is all that dangerous, either.

“It was instincts, and once you see the run and the linebacker got upfield, so I had to make a cut, then I was just me,” Irving said of that play. “I already [told] myself that once I trust my track, good things happen. That was just me trusting my track. I got back on my track when I was supposed to hit it.”

Whether this represents Irving and the Bucs’ offense getting back on track is another matter, but it was a good week for a formerly 0-4 team.

Christian Watson, WR, Green Bay Packers

Life is always better in the NFC North when the Green Bay Packers and the Chicago Bears legitimately dislike each other, and with the beefs between Packers head coach Matt LaFleur and Bears head coach Ben Johnson, that’s now the case. Sunday’s game was the latest instance of the NFL’s longest-running rivalry, and this one wasn’t really competitive. The Packers blew the Bears right out of Lambeau Field with a 31-7 win, and quarterback Jordan Love was slinging the ball like there was no tomorrow.

In the first four weeks of the season, Love had completed four of 18 passes of 20 or more air yards for 144 yards, no touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 37.3. But against the Bears, Love completed six of eight deep passes for 258 yards (32.3 yards per attempt!), two touchdowns, no interceptions, and a passer rating of 156.3, which is absolutely and utterly ridiculous.

The key man in Love’s goal to push the ball down the field was receiver Christian Watson, who caught three of those deep passes on four targets for 126 yards and both touchdowns. The first score, a 42-yarder, came with 5:57 left in the first quarter. Watson motioned from right to left pre-snap, took off at the snap up the seam, and the Bears didn’t seem to know what to do with that. Safety Xavier Woods got caught up in the wash, and that was that.

Then, the Packers opened the second half with a full “F**K YOU” playbook, in which Love was going to attempt to embarrass Chicago’s defense deep until it stuck.

With 13:33 left in the third quarter, there was the deep incompletion to Watson on the left boundary that probably should have been pass interference on cornerback Tyrique Stevenson. Then, there was the deep pass to receiver J. Michael Sturdivant which was negated by offensive pass interference — a call the Packers very much did not enjoy. Finally, the 53-yard touchdown to Watson with 13:19 left in the quarter.

Quite a statement against a Bears defense that had allowed a grand total of six deep catches on 10 targets for 243 yards, two touchdowns, one interception, and an opponent passer rating of 104.2 in the first four weeks.

“You know, I think J-Mike did a great job making that catch, and it’s one of those things, it is what it is,” Love said of that particular sequence. “It’s unfortunate, got called back, but it’s what we always talk about. How do you respond? It’s adversity, you never know when it’s going to hit. To be able to go get that one to Christian (Watson), that huge play, I thought he did an outstanding job making that catch, but that’s what it’s all about right there.

“I said, ‘Ball don’t lie.'”

Ball don’t lie, and at least in this game, the truth was that Christian Watson was the Packers’ nuclear option whenever it was time for an explosive play.

Renardo Green, CB, San Francisco 49ers

The last time we checked in on 49ers cornerback Renardo Green, he was in Kyle Shanahan’s doghouse during San Francisco’s Divisional Round loss to the Seattle Seahawks last season, and hoping that Raheem Morris’ new set of defensive schemes would bring out the best in him.

I had my eye on Green from his time at Florida State, because I love me a good press cornerback, the Seminoles played a metric crapton of press when Green was there, and Green was really, really good at it.

But the transitions didn’t always play at the next level. The 49ers took Green in the second round of the 2024 draft, and he was up and down at best in his first two seasons, allowing 81 catches on 141 targets for 938 yards, five touchdowns, one interception, and an opponent passer rating of 86.5.

Now, in Morris’ schemes, Green is starting to get the hang of everything. This was never more evident than in San Francisco’s 32-29 Sunday win over the Seahawks. The first time Green faced Seattle since last season’s dressing-down, he was as good as anybody could have hoped. Green was Sam Darnold’s worst nightmare, allowing two catches on five targets for five yards, no touchdowns, two interceptions, a pass breakup, and an opponent passer rating of 8.3.

Green was on Darnold’s reads from the jump, and it was impressive that he did it in multiple ways — he’s not just a press guy anymore.

Moreover, Green is taking his film study to the field in new ways. His description of how he set Darnold up with his second interception of the day on a Darnold target to tight end Elijah Arroyo with 14:18 left in the third quarter was specifically impressive.

From ESPN’s Nick Wagoner:

“It was a double tight end formation and one of them [Arroyo] released… You [can] run past him. So when he ran the over route, I played like he had a step on me. Once the ball went in the air, I just turned it on, and undercut the ball.”

Green also undercut Darnold’s throw to Jaxon Smith-Njigba with 12:40 left in the first quarter on a quick out route. Anytime you can get the best of the NFL’s best receiver, you’re doing some stuff. Green also knocked the snot out of JSN on his pass breakup with 1:13 left in the game — a play that helped decide things near the end.

Despite all the attendant and seemingly inevitable injuries, the 49ers are 5-0 on the season, and they’re absolutely crushing everyone else in the DVOA sweepstakes. It’s nice that Green is a big part of the equation after a rocky start to his career.
